Conventions.
• "separation A -> B over R" means B ≰_R A; "implication A -> B over R" means B ≤_R A (database convention).
• CMV = [@ciprianimarconevalenti2022] (arXiv:2210.15556v2), KMP = [@kiharamarconepauly2020], GPV = [@gohpaulyvalenti2021], Goh = [@goh2020b].
• All Cantor–Bendixson problems here are *not ω-absolute*: every fact below is a fact about true instances and
true solutions (reductions sW, W, c, aW, cW). **No ω-model or RCA₀ fact is claimed anywhere in this file.**
• Names. A closed set of ℕ^ℕ (resp. 2^ℕ) is named by any tree T ⊆ ℕ^{<ℕ} (resp. binary tree) with [T] equal to it

(CMV, Section 2.2, "tree representation", stated to be equivalent to the negative representation). A name of PK_X(A) is therefore *any* tree U with [U] = PK(A), not necessarily pruned. A Σ¹₁ (Π¹₁) code of A ⊆ ℕ is, up to computable translation, a sequence of trees (T_n) with n ∈ A iff T_n ill-founded (well-founded).
• Classical facts used without further reference (all in Sacks, *Higher recursion theory*, or Moschovakis,
*Descriptive set theory*), in relativized form:
• (GB) Gandy basis theorem: a nonempty Σ¹₁(Z) class of reals has a member p with ω₁^{p⊕Z} = ω₁^Z.
• (BD) Σ¹₁-boundedness: a Σ¹₁(Y) set of (indices of) Y-computable well-founded trees has ranks bounded below ω₁^Y.
• (UN) Π¹₁ number-uniformization: every Π¹₁(Z) relation R ⊆ ℕ×ℕ has a Π¹₁(Z) subrelation R* with the same
domain that is the graph of a function.
• (SG) Spector–Gandy: "∃y ∈ Δ¹₁(Z) φ(y)" with φ arithmetical is Π¹₁(Z).
• (EP) effective perfect set theorem: every member of a countable Σ¹₁(Z) class is Δ¹₁(Z).
• (CB) the perfect kernel of a closed set A of a Polish space is its set of condensation points; hence, for
A = [S] ⊆ ℕ^ℕ, with E_S := {σ : A ∩ [σ] is countable}: PK(A) = {x : ∀m x↾m ∉ E_S}, Sc(A) = {x ∈ A : ∃m x↾m ∈ E_S}, and E_S is Π¹₁(S) (CMV Theorem 2.11(ii)) and closed under extensions.
• (HA) there is a computable linear order (a Harrison order) that is ill-founded and has no hyperarithmetic
descending sequence (GPV, proof of Proposition 4.2, citing Sacks III.2.1); relativizes to any oracle.

blocks.label: Theorem 1
blocks.text: Let Z ⊆ ℕ, let S be a Z-computable tree, A = [S] ⊆ ℕ^ℕ, and let C ⊆ ℕ^ℕ be a (boldface) closed set with no Δ¹₁(Z) element. Then there is a solution Y = (U, (b_i, x_i)_i, n) ∈ CB_ℕᴺ(A) such that Z ⊕ Y computes no element of C.
proof: Write the proof for Z = ∅ (it relativizes verbatim). Let T_C be the tree of C, E := E_S, n_A the correct value of ScCount(A).

steps: *Hyperarithmetic scattered points.* If x ∈ Sc(A), some x↾m ∈ E, so x belongs to the countable Π⁰₁ class A ∩ [x↾m] and x is hyperarithmetic by (EP).

*The set V := {σ : [σ] ∩ Sc(A) ≠ ∅} is Π¹₁.* Indeed σ ∈ V iff ∃σ′ ⊇ σ (σ′ ∈ E ∧ ∃y ∈ HYP (σ′ ≺ y ∧ y ∈ [S])). (⇒: take x ∈ Sc(A) ∩ [σ], m ≥ |σ| with x↾m ∈ E (E is closed under extensions), σ′ = x↾m, y = x, hyperarithmetic by step 1. ⇐: y ∈ A ∩ [σ′] with σ′ ∈ E, so y ∈ Sc(A) by (CB).) The right-hand side is Π¹₁ by (SG) and because E is Π¹₁.

*Conditions.* A condition is p = (τ, (b_i, σ_i, y_i)_{i<k}) where τ is a finite sequence of elements of E ∪ {⋆}; b_i ∈ {0,1}; σ_i ∈ ℕ^{<ℕ}, y_i ∈ ℕ^ℕ, σ_i ≺ y_i; if b_i = 1 then y_i ∈ Sc(A); if b_i = 0 then y_i = 0^ℕ. p′ extends p if τ′ ⊇ τ, k′ ≥ k, and for i < k: b′_i = b_i, y′_i = y_i, σ′_i ⊇ σ_i. The *finite part* of p is fp(p) := (τ, (b_i, σ_i)_{i<k}).

*The solution attached to a generic sequence.* Let p_0 ≥ p_1 ≥ … be a sequence of conditions meeting the dense sets (a) {p : σ ∈ range(τ)} for each σ ∈ E; (b) {p : ∃i (b_i = 1 ∧ y_i = y)} for each y ∈ Sc(A) (countably many, Sc(A) is countable); (c) {p : k > i ∧ |σ_i| ≥ m ∧ |τ| ≥ m} for all i, m; (d) the sets D_e of step 6. Let g := ⋃τ : ℕ → E ∪ {⋆}, x_i := y_i, and U_g := {σ ∈ ℕ^{<ℕ} : no prefix of σ is among g(0), …, g(|σ|−1)}. U_g is a tree containing ⟨⟩, and x ∈ [U_g] iff no prefix of x lies in range(g) = E iff x ∈ PK(A) by (CB). By (b), {x_i : b_i = 1} = Sc(A). So Y_g := (U_g, (b_i, x_i)_i, n_A) ∈ CB_ℕᴺ(A).

*Finite parts.* For every m, the restriction of (the standard name of) Y_g to arguments < m is determined by fp(p_j) for j large (the membership of σ in U_g depends on g↾|σ| only; n_A is a constant). For a Turing functional Φ_e write Φ_e^{fp(p)} for the finite string computed by Φ_e from the part of the oracle determined by fp(p) in at most |τ| steps; it is monotone in p.
*Dense sets.* Bad_e := {p : Φ_e^{fp(p)} ∉ T_C} ∪ {p : ∃n ∀p′ ≤ p Φ_e^{fp(p′)}(n)↑}, D_e := Bad_e ∪ {p : no extension of p is in Bad_e}. D_e is dense.

Suppose Φ_e^{Y_g} ∈ C. Then no p_j is in Bad_e (first part: Φ_e^{Y_g} would have a prefix outside T_C; second part: Φ_e^{Y_g}(n) would be undefined). As the sequence meets D_e, some p* := p_j has no extension in Bad_e.

Let F := {fp(p) : p ≤ p*}. With p* = (τ*, (b*_i, σ*_i, y*_i)_{i<k*}), a finite object (τ, (b_i, σ_i)_{i<k}) is in F iff: τ ⊇ τ* with all entries in E ∪ {⋆}; k ≥ k*; for i < k*: b_i = b*_i and σ*_i ⊆ σ_i ≺ y*_i; for k* ≤ i < k: if b_i = 1 then σ_i ∈ V, if b_i = 0 then σ_i ≺ 0^ℕ. (For ⇐ choose y_i ∈ Sc(A) ∩ [σ_i].) The y*_i are hyperarithmetic (step 1) or 0^ℕ, E and V are Π¹₁ (step 2), so **F is Π¹₁**.

Let Q := {ρ ∈ ℕ^{<ℕ} : ∃φ ∈ F (ρ ⊆ Φ_e^φ)}. Then: Q is Π¹₁ (number quantifier over a Π¹₁ set); ⟨⟩ ∈ Q; Q is closed under prefixes; Q ⊆ T_C (no extension of p* is in the first part of Bad_e, and T_C is a tree); every ρ ∈ Q has some ρ⌢k ∈ Q (if ρ ⊆ Φ_e^{fp(p)}, p ≤ p*, then p is not in the second part of Bad_e for n = |ρ|, so some p′ ≤ p has Φ_e^{fp(p′)}(|ρ|)↓, and ρ ⊆ Φ_e^{fp(p′)} by monotonicity).

*A hyperarithmetic path.* R(ρ, k) :⇔ ρ⌢k ∈ Q is Π¹₁ with domain Q. Let R* be given by (UN). Define "σ ≺ y" :⇔ ∀i < |σ| R*(σ↾i, σ(i)), a Π¹₁ predicate. By induction on length exactly one σ of each length satisfies it and it lies in Q; so y ∈ [Q] is well defined, and y(n) = k ⇔ ∃σ of length n+1 with σ ≺ y and σ(n) = k ⇔ ¬∃σ of length n+1 with σ ≺ y and σ(n) ≠ k. The graph of y is Δ¹₁, so y is hyperarithmetic, and y ∈ [Q] ⊆ [T_C] = C: contradiction with the hypothesis on C.
Hence no Φ_e maps Y_g into C: Y_g computes no element of C.

DS ≰_c CB_ℕᴺ. Let H be the order of (HA). If DS ≤_c CB_ℕᴺ, there is a computable S such that every Y ∈ CB_ℕᴺ([S]) computes (with the computable H) an element of the closed set C := DS(H), which has no hyperarithmetic element: contradiction with [#Theorem 1]. Since DS ≤_W C_ℕᴺ ≤_W TC_ℕᴺ, also C_ℕᴺ, TC_ℕᴺ ≰_c CB_ℕᴺ.

ATR₂ ≰_c CB_ℕᴺ. Let (L, B) be a computable instance of ATR₂ with no hyperarithmetic solution (Goh Corollary 8.7). Let C be the set of 0⌢s with s ∈ DS(L), together with 1⌢(X ⊕ h) where X = ⟨X_a⟩_{a∈L}, X_{0_L} = B, and for all b >_L 0_L and n: (n ∈ X_b → the n-th computation with oracle ⊕_{a<b}X_a halts within h(b,n) steps) and (n ∉ X_b → that computation never halts). C is closed (Π⁰₁ in L ⊕ B). Every ATR₂-solution computes an element of C (for a jump hierarchy X, let h(b,n) be the halting time if n ∈ X_b, found by search, and 0 otherwise), and every element of C computes an ATR₂-solution; so C has no hyperarithmetic element. Apply [#Theorem 1].

χ_Π¹₁^ ≰_c CB_ℕᴺ (hence PK ≰_c CB_ℕᴺ, as PK ≡_sW χ_Π¹₁^, CMV Theorem 4.2). Let (T_e) be a computable sequence of trees with W := {e : T_e ∈ WF} Π¹₁-complete; the unique solution χ_W is not hyperarithmetic and C := {χ_W} is closed. Apply [#Theorem 1].

Weihrauch reductions are computable reductions, so none of DS, C_ℕᴺ, TC_ℕᴺ, ATR₂ is Weihrauch reducible to CB_ℕᴺ, nor to anything below it. For cW: a reduction relative to an oracle Z is refuted by [#Theorem 1] relative to Z (using the relativizations of (HA), of Goh Corollary 8.7 — the argument of its proof relativizes —, and of the completeness of W).

items.dependencies: (CB), (UN), (SG), (EP), (HA) above; Goh Corollary 8.7 (ATR₂ has a computable instance with no hyperarithmetic solution); CMV Theorem 2.11(ii); for the listed consequences, CMV Theorems 4.32(iii), 4.35; GPV Proposition 4.2 (DS ≤_W C_ℕᴺ).
items.concerns: this is (CB), valid for every closed A, including A = ℕ^ℕ (E = ∅, g ≡ ⋆) and A countable (U_g well-founded, a legitimate name of ∅ since it contains ⟨⟩). The list part needs the b_i = 0 entries to be harmless: Definition 4.15 only constrains {x_i : b_i = 1}. (ii) *Weakest point: the complexity of F.* A naive "σ extends to a scattered point" is Σ¹₁; step 2 replaces it by a Π¹₁ statement using that scattered points are hyperarithmetic and (SG). Without this the set Q would only be Σ¹₁ and the theorem would be false in general (Ext(T) is a Σ¹₁ pruned subtree of T). (iii) *Why Π¹₁ suffices:* a Π¹₁ pruned tree has a hyperarithmetic path by (UN) (step 10); this is exactly where the analogous statement for Σ¹₁ trees fails. (iv) *Sanity checks:* the theorem is consistent with UC_ℕᴺ ≤_W PK_ℕᴺ (CMV Proposition 4.12: the closed set is a hyperarithmetic singleton), with Σ¹₁-C_ℕ ≤_W CB_ℕᴺ (Section 2: solutions are numbers), and with C_ℕᴺ ≤_W χ_Π¹₁^: a *characteristic function* of a Π¹₁-complete set computes paths, an *enumeration* of it (which is all a name of PK(A) gives) does not. (v) The direction: the fact says cnn ≰ cb-baire, i.e. "separation from cb-baire to cnn".

steps: Given (T_n), let R_n := {⟨⟩} ∪ {⟨m⟩⌢τ : m ≤ n, τ ∈ T_m}; R_n is ill-founded iff some T_m, m ≤ n, is.
Let G_n := Expl(R_n) = R_n ∗ 2^{<ℕ} (CMV Section 2.1): well-founded iff R_n is; if R_n is ill-founded, [G_n] = {p ∗ q : p ∈ [R_n], q ∈ 2^ℕ} is nonempty without isolated points.

Let U_n := {0^k : k ∈ ℕ} ∪ {0^k⌢1⌢τ : k ∈ ℕ, τ ∈ G_n}, so [U_n] = {0^ℕ} ∪ {0^k 1 x : x ∈ [G_n]}. If R_n is well-founded, [U_n] = {0^ℕ}. If not, [U_n] is closed without isolated points (0^ℕ = lim_k 0^k 1 x₀).

Let S := {⟨⟩} ∪ {⟨n⟩⌢τ : τ ∈ U_n}, A := [S]. Each A ∩ [⟨n⟩] is clopen in A. If R_n is well-founded it is the isolated point n0^ℕ, which is in Sc(A). If R_n is ill-founded it is a perfect subset of A, hence inside PK(A). So Sc(A) = {n0^ℕ : R_n well-founded} = {n0^ℕ : n < n*}, n* := the least n with T_n ill-founded (∞ if none).
Hence ScCount(A) = 0 if all T_n are well-founded and n*+1 otherwise: exactly LeastIF_⊥((T_n)). The backward map is the identity on the answer, so the reduction is strong.

blocks.label: (b) ScCount_ℕᴺ ≤_sW LeastIF_⊥
proof: Given a tree T, compute trees T_n (n ∈ ℕ) with T_n well-founded iff

ϕ(n+1, T) (Remark 4.28, Π¹₁ uniformly). ϕ(n, T) is decreasing in n, and |Sc([T])| ≥ n iff ϕ(n, T). So the least n with T_n ill-founded is |Sc([T])|, and there is none iff Sc([T]) is infinite: LeastIF_⊥((T_n)) = ScCount([T]).

blocks.label: (c) Σ¹₁-C_ℕ ≤_sW ScCount_ℕᴺ
proof: An instance is (T_n) with some T_n ill-founded; by (a) ScCount(A) − 1 is the

least such n. As ScList_ℕᴺ and CB_ℕᴺ output ScCount(A) as a component, Σ¹₁-C_ℕ ≤_sW ScList_ℕᴺ, CB_ℕᴺ. (In the same way the *least* element of a nonempty Π¹₁ set is computed: for (T_i) with some T_i well-founded, let P_i :⇔ T_i ∈ WF ∧ ∀i′ < i (T_{i′} ∈ IF ∨ rk T_i < rk T_{i′}), a Π¹₁ statement; the i with P_i have strictly decreasing ranks, so they are finitely many, and the least of them is the least well-founded index; take 2^i trees equivalent to P_i for each i and read the lowest binary digit of the count.)
**(d) C_ℕ ≰_W χ_Π¹₁^*, hence ScCount_ℕᴺ ≰_W χ_Π¹₁^*.**

steps: Suppose C_ℕ ≤_W χ_Π¹₁^* via Φ, Ψ. An instance of C_ℕ is an enumeration p of the complement of a nonempty set (p(i) = n+1 removes n, p(i) = 0 removes nothing). Let p₀ := 0^ℕ. Φ(p₀) is a number k and k trees; k is determined by a prefix p₀↾u.

Build p_0, p_1, … , answers n_i and bit vectors b^i ∈ 2^k: b^i is the vector of χ_Π¹₁-answers for Φ(p_i), n_i := Ψ(p_i, b^i) with use u_i ≥ u on p_i, and p_{i+1} := p_i↾u_i ⌢ (n_i + 1) ⌢ 0^ℕ. Each p_i removes only n_0, …, n_{i−1}, so it is an instance, and it extends p_j↾u_j for all j < i (so Φ(p_i) has the same k).
If b^i = b^j for some j < i then Ψ(p_i, b^i) = Ψ(p_j↾u_j …, b^j) = n_j, which p_i removes: wrong. So b^0, b^1, … are pairwise distinct elements of 2^k: impossible after 2^k + 1 steps.

C_ℕ ≤_sW Σ¹₁-C_ℕ (a Π⁰₁ set is Σ¹₁) ≤_sW ScCount_ℕᴺ by (c). So ScCount_ℕᴺ ≰_W χ_Π¹₁^*. **(e) χ_Π¹₁^{u*} ≰_W ScCount_ℕᴺ.** Let f be the first-order problem: an instance is a sequence of pairs of trees (a_n, b_n)_n such that some n has a_n ∈ WF and b_n ∈ IF; a solution is such an n.
f ≤_W χ_Π¹₁^ (ask about all a_n, b_n and search), f is first-order, so f ≤_W χ_Π¹₁^{u*} (Theorems 2.13, 2.14). It suffices to show f ≰_W ScCount_ℕᴺ.

Suppose f ≤_W ScCount_ℕᴺ via Φ, Ψ. For an index e let C(e, k) :⇔ "φ_e is total, Φ^{φ_e} is (the characteristic function of) a tree T, and ϕ(k, T)": a Π¹₁ predicate of (e, k), decreasing in k. Let g_e(κ) := the number output by Ψ(φ_e, κ̄) for κ ∈ ℕ ∪ {∞}, where κ̄ is the ScCount-code of κ (0 for ∞, κ+1 otherwise); g_e is partial computable uniformly in e.
By the uniform normal form for Π¹₁ predicates of numbers there is a total computable h such that φ_{h(e)} is (a name of) the sequence (a_n, b_n)_n with

proof: • a_0, a_1 well-founded iff ∀k C(e, k); a_n := {⟨⟩} for n ≥ 2;
• b_i (i = 0, 1) well-founded iff ∀k C(e, k) ∧ g_e(∞)↓ = i;
• b_n (n ≥ 2) well-founded iff ∃k ∈ ℕ (g_e(k)↓ = n ∧ C(e, k)) ∨ (∀k C(e, k) ∧ g_e(∞)↓ = n).
All right-hand sides are Π¹₁ in (e, n). Fix e with φ_e = φ_{h(e)} =: x by the recursion theorem.

steps: Let c := sup{k : C(e, k)} ∈ {−1} ∪ ℕ ∪ {∞} (−1 if C(e, 0) fails, i.e. Φ(x) is not a tree). *Case c ∈ {−1} ∪ ℕ.* Then a_0, a_1 ∈ IF, so 0, 1 are not solutions; for n ≥ 2, a_n ∈ WF and b_n ∈ WF iff n ∈ g_e({0, …, c}), a finite set. So some n ≥ 2 is a solution: x ∈ dom(f). Hence Φ(x) names a closed set, c ≥ 0, |Sc| = c (Remark 4.28), ScCount = c̄, and g_e(c) = Ψ(x, c̄) must be a solution. But g_e(c) ∈ {0, 1} is not a solution, and g_e(c) = n ≥ 2 makes b_n well-founded (witness k = c): contradiction. *Case c = ∞.* Then a_0, a_1 ∈ WF, and ScCount of Φ(x) is 0̄ = code of ∞ once x ∈ dom(f). If g_e(∞) = 0: b_0 ∈ WF, b_1 ∈ IF, so 1 is a solution (x ∈ dom(f)) and the answer 0 is not. Symmetrically if g_e(∞) = 1. Otherwise b_0, b_1 ∈ IF, so 0 and 1 are solutions and x ∈ dom(f); then g_e(∞)↓ = n ≥ 2 and b_n ∈ WF by the second disjunct: n is not a solution. Contradiction in every case.

blocks: Note to Section 1 (relativization for ATR₂). For the cW version of step 13 one does not need Goh's Corollary 8.7: for any Z let H^Z be the Harrison order relative to Z. A jump hierarchy on H^Z starting with Z restricts, on the well-founded initial segment (of type ω₁^Z), to the true hierarchy by transfinite induction, so it computes every Δ¹₁(Z) set and is not Δ¹₁(Z); and H^Z has no Δ¹₁(Z) descending sequence. So (H^Z, Z) is a Z-computable instance of ATR₂ with no Δ¹₁(Z) solution.

items.concerns: the only delicate point is that kernel and scattered part are computed piecewise on a clopen partition: a perfect subset of a clopen piece is a perfect subset of A; a point isolated in A is not in any perfect subset. Checked. Remark 4.28 is used exactly as CMV use it in Theorem 4.29. (ii) (e) is a diagonalization through the recursion theorem; the weakest point is that every clause defining the instance must be Π¹₁ *in e* although it speaks about the truth of the count of Φ(x): "count ≥ k" is Π¹₁ (this is what distinguishes ScCount from χ_Π¹₁^{u*}, where "the answer is k" is only Π¹₁ ∧ Σ¹₁), "count = ∞" is Π¹₁, and the clauses use only these. That x ∈ dom(f) is proved in each case *before* using that Ψ answers correctly, from the value c defined by the formula alone. The two reserve candidates 0, 1 are needed for the case c = ∞ (with one reserve the reduction "answer the reserve when the count is infinite" would win). (iii) Sanity check against (c): the diagonal instance is not of the special forms (Σ¹₁ choice, least Π¹₁ element) for which reductions exist, and running the diagonal against the reduction of (c) breaks at "x ∈ dom". (iv) (d) is the standard argument that C_ℕ is not reducible to a problem answering with boundedly many bits.

steps: (X = ∅ for notation.) DS(L) is a nonempty closed subset of ℕ^ℕ, so a Polish space. With C_e := {s ∈ DS(L) : Φ_e^s = p}, DS(L) = ⋃_e C_e. By the Baire category theorem some C_e is dense in a nonempty relatively open set [σ₀] ∩ DS(L) (σ₀ a finite descending sequence; we may take σ₀ ≠ ⟨⟩).

Call a finite descending sequence F *extendible* if [F] ∩ DS(L) ≠ ∅, i.e. if there is an infinite descending sequence below last(F). (i) If F ⊇ σ₀ is extendible and Φ_e^F(n)↓ then Φ_e^F(n) = p(n) (some s ∈ C_e extends F). (ii) For every n some extendible F ⊇ σ₀ has Φ_e^F(n)↓ (a prefix of some s ∈ C_e ∩ [σ₀]).

Fix n. At stage t let Cand_t be the set of finite descending sequences F ⊇ σ₀ with entries and length < t such that Φ_e^F(n) halts in < t steps; if Cand_t ≠ ∅ let F_t ∈ Cand_t have the <_L-largest last element

proof: and v_t := Φ_e^{F_t}(n).

blocks.label: (a) Lemma A
blocks.text: If lim ≤_W g and g ∗ g ≤_W g, then f ≤_aW g implies f ≤_W g.

steps: Let Φ(p) = φ(p⁽ⁿ⁾) and Ψ(p, q) = ψ((p ⊕ q)⁽ⁿ⁾) with φ, ψ computable. Then f is refined by h₃ ∘ h₂ ∘ h₁ with h₁(p) = (p, φ(p⁽ⁿ⁾)) ≤_W lim^{[n]}, h₂(p, z) = {p} × g(z) ≤_W g, h₃(p, q) = ψ((p ⊕ q)⁽ⁿ⁾) ≤_W lim^{[n]}.
So f ≤_W lim^{[n]} ∗ g ∗ lim^{[n]} ≤_W g ∗ ⋯ ∗ g ≤_W g.
Apply Lemma A to g = C_ℕᴺ: χ_Π¹₁ ≰_aW C_ℕᴺ since χ_Π¹₁ ≰_W C_ℕᴺ. Apply it to g = UC_ℕᴺ: Σ¹₁-C_ℕ ≰_aW UC_ℕᴺ and DS ≰_aW UC_ℕᴺ since they are not Weihrauch reducible to UC_ℕᴺ.

blocks.label: (b) Lemma B
blocks.text: If every arithmetical instance of g has an arithmetical solution and f has a computable instance with no arithmetical solution, then f ≰_aW g. (Φ of the instance is arithmetical, Ψ of an arithmetical solution is arithmetical.)

steps: UC_ℕᴺ has a computable instance whose solution is not arithmetical: apply the reduction ATR ≤_W UC_ℕᴺ (KMP Theorem 3.13) to the computable instance (ω, ∅) of ATR, whose solution computes ∅^{(n)} for all n.

Call σ ∈ 2^{<ℕ} consistent if (σ(m), σ(m′)) ∈ g(m, m′) for all m < m′ < |σ|. The consistent strings form a tree 𝒯 that is c.e. in Z, and D↾n ∈ 𝒯 for all n.

No level of 𝒯 has three elements: if σ₁, σ₂, σ₃ are distinct of the same length, pick m with σ₁(m) ≠ σ₂(m); σ₃ agrees at m with one of them, say σ₁; pick m′ with σ₃(m′) ≠ σ₁(m′). The three pairs (σ_i(m), σ_i(m′)) are pairwise distinct, so g has ≥ 3 elements at {m, m′}: contradiction.

So 𝒯 is a binary tree with at most two paths. Ext := {σ ∈ 𝒯 : ∀n ≥ |σ| ∃τ ⊇ σ (|τ| = n ∧ τ ∈ 𝒯)} is Π⁰₂(Z) and is the set of prefixes of paths (König). D is the unique path, or one of two paths splitting at a level ℓ; in both cases D↾n is the unique element of Ext of length n extending D↾(ℓ+1), so D ≤_T Ext ≤_T Z″. Then D is arithmetical: contradiction.

steps: Let E := {i : T_i ∈ WF}. A *condition* is a finite sequence c = (ρ_i)_{i<k} of finite strings; it is *valid* if for all i < k: ρ_i ∉ {0}^* ⇒ i ∈ E. Validity is Π¹₁(p).

For a condition c and e ∈ ℕ let Q(c, e) :⇔ ∃c′ ⊇ c (c′ valid ∧ Φ_e^{p⊕c′}(e)↓ using only the part of the oracle determined by c′). Q is Π¹₁(p), uniformly; so there are trees R_{c,e}, computable from p uniformly, with R_{c,e} ∈ WF ⇔ Q(c, e). Let Φ*(p) := ((T_i)_i, (R_{c,e})_{c,e}).

Ψ*: from the answers we know χ_E and all Q(c, e). Build c_0 ⊆ c_1 ⊆ … : c_0 := ∅. Given c_e (valid): if Q(c_e, e), search for the first c′ ⊇ c_e which is valid (decidable from χ_E) with Φ_e^{p⊕c′}(e)↓; put e in K; otherwise c′ := c_e and e ∉ K. Then let c_{e+1} be c′ with a 0 appended to every ρ_i, with empty strings added so that ρ_0, …, ρ_e exist, and, if e ∈ E and ρ_e ∈ {0}^*, with a 1 appended to ρ_e. c_{e+1} is valid (appending 0s and empty strings preserves validity; a 1 is appended only for e ∈ E).
Let q_i := ⋃_e ρ_i, y := (q_i)_i. Each q_i is total. If q_i ≠ 0^ℕ then i ∈ E (validity); if i ∈ E then q_i ≠ 0^ℕ (stage i). So y names an element of WF_S^((T_i)_i).

K = (p ⊕ y)′: if Q(c_e, e), the computation converges on c_{e+1} ⊆ y. If not, and Φ_e^{p⊕y}(e)↓, a finite part c′ ⊇ c_e of y would witness Q(c_e, e) (every finite part of y is valid by step 4): contradiction.

blocks.label: Theorem 11
blocks.text: If f₁ ≤_W lim and g₁ ≤_W WF_S^, then f₁ ∘ g₁ ≤_W WF^. Hence lim ∗ PK_ℕᴺ ≤_W WF^ ≡_W PK.

steps: Let (Φ₁, Ψ₁) witness f₁ ≤_W lim and (Φ₂, Ψ₂) witness g₁ ≤_W WF_S^. Let x be (a name of) an instance of f₁ ∘ g₁: x ∈ dom(g₁) and g₁(x) ⊆ dom(f₁). (T_i)_i := Φ₂(x) is computable from x.
Apply [#Lemma 11] with p := x: from the WF^-answers to Φ*(x) compute y, a name of an element of WF_S^(Φ₂(x)), and K = (x ⊕ y)′.

w := Ψ₂(x, y) is a name of an element of g₁(x) ⊆ dom(f₁), computable from x ⊕ y. Φ₁(w) is a convergent sequence computable from x ⊕ y; its limit ℓ is computable from K (for each n search the least s₀ such that the Π⁰₁(x ⊕ y) statement "∀s ≥ s₀ the s-th term agrees with the s₀-th up to n" holds, which K decides).
Ψ₁(w, ℓ) is a name of an element of f₁(δ(w)) ⊆ (f₁ ∘ g₁)(x). All steps are uniform in x and the answers: f₁ ∘ g₁ ≤_W WF^.
lim ∗ PK_ℕᴺ ≡_W lim ∗ WF_S^ (Theorem 4.9; ∗ is monotone) is the maximum of such f₁ ∘ g₁, so it is ≤_W WF^ ≡_W PK (Theorem 4.2). With Theorem 4.11: PK ≡_W lim ∗ PK_ℕᴺ.

items.dependencies: CMV Theorem 4.9 (PK_ℕᴺ ≡_W WF_S^), Theorem 4.2 (WF^ ≡_sW PK), Theorem 4.11 (PK ≤_W lim ∗ PK_ℕᴺ); the uniform Π¹₁ normal form (CMV Theorem 2.11(i): WF is Π¹₁-complete for effective Wadge reducibility); lim ≡_sW J (CMV Section 4.1, citing [@brattkadebrechtpauly2012] Lemma 8.9), used only in the form "the limit of a convergent sequence computable in w is computable in w′, uniformly".
items.concerns: * a solution of WF^ has a unique name, whose jump is the jump of the hyperjump; a solution of WF_S^ has many names and Lemma 11 picks a 1-generic one, whose jump is computable from the hyperjump. The composition f₁ ∘ g₁ only has to answer for *one* element of g₁(x), which is what a realizer does. (ii) *Weakest point: the domain condition.* f₁ ∘ g₁ is defined at x only if *every* element of g₁(x) lies in dom(f₁); the name y of Lemma 11 names an element of WF_S^(Φ₂(x)), so Ψ₂(x, y) names an element of g₁(x), and Φ₁ of it converges. Deciding Σ⁰₂(p ⊕ y) facts would need "∀ valid c″", which is Σ¹₁ inside a Π¹₁ matrix: the argument does not give lim ∗ lim ∗ PK_ℕᴺ ≤_W WF^, as it should not be expected to. (iv) The questions Q(c, e) are asked for all c in advance, including invalid ones; only the answers for the c_e actually reached are used. (v) Strings: a finite part ρ_i ∈ {0}^* is compatible both with q_i = 0^ℕ and with q_i ≠ 0^ℕ, so valid conditions with i ∈ E and ρ_i ∈ {0}^* are fine; step 3 makes ρ_i nonzero at stage i.

Conventions.
• "separation A -> B over R" means B ≰_R A; "implication A -> B over R" means B ≤_R A (database convention).
• CMV = [@ciprianimarconevalenti2022] (arXiv:2210.15556v2), KMP = [@kiharamarconepauly2020], GPV = [@gohpaulyvalenti2021], Goh = [@goh2020b].
• All Cantor–Bendixson problems here are *not ω-absolute*: every fact below is a fact about true instances and
true solutions (reductions sW, W, c, aW, cW). **No ω-model or RCA₀ fact is claimed anywhere in this file.**
• Names. A closed set of ℕ^ℕ (resp. 2^ℕ) is named by any tree T ⊆ ℕ^{<ℕ} (resp. binary tree) with [T] equal to it

(CMV, Section 2.2, "tree representation", stated to be equivalent to the negative representation). A name of PK_X(A) is therefore *any* tree U with [U] = PK(A), not necessarily pruned. A Σ¹₁ (Π¹₁) code of A ⊆ ℕ is, up to computable translation, a sequence of trees (T_n) with n ∈ A iff T_n ill-founded (well-founded).
• Classical facts used without further reference (all in Sacks, *Higher recursion theory*, or Moschovakis,
*Descriptive set theory*), in relativized form:
• (GB) Gandy basis theorem: a nonempty Σ¹₁(Z) class of reals has a member p with ω₁^{p⊕Z} = ω₁^Z.
• (BD) Σ¹₁-boundedness: a Σ¹₁(Y) set of (indices of) Y-computable well-founded trees has ranks bounded below ω₁^Y.
• (UN) Π¹₁ number-uniformization: every Π¹₁(Z) relation R ⊆ ℕ×ℕ has a Π¹₁(Z) subrelation R* with the same
domain that is the graph of a function.
• (SG) Spector–Gandy: "∃y ∈ Δ¹₁(Z) φ(y)" with φ arithmetical is Π¹₁(Z).
• (EP) effective perfect set theorem: every member of a countable Σ¹₁(Z) class is Δ¹₁(Z).
• (CB) the perfect kernel of a closed set A of a Polish space is its set of condensation points; hence, for
A = [S] ⊆ ℕ^ℕ, with E_S := {σ : A ∩ [σ] is countable}: PK(A) = {x : ∀m x↾m ∉ E_S}, Sc(A) = {x ∈ A : ∃m x↾m ∈ E_S}, and E_S is Π¹₁(S) (CMV Theorem 2.11(ii)) and closed under extensions.
• (HA) there is a computable linear order (a Harrison order) that is ill-founded and has no hyperarithmetic
descending sequence (GPV, proof of Proposition 4.2, citing Sacks III.2.1); relativizes to any oracle.

blocks.label: Proof
proof: Let S be a tree, A = [S].

steps: Ctb := {σ : A ∩ [σ] is countable and nonempty} is Π¹₁ in S, uniformly: for countable A ∩ [σ], nonemptiness is equivalent to ∃y ∈ Δ¹₁(S) (y ∈ [S] ∩ [σ]) by (EP), which is Π¹₁ by (SG). So there are trees D_σ, computable from (S, σ), with D_σ ∈ WF ⇔ σ ∈ Ctb.
Let P(σ) :⇔ D_σ ∈ WF ∧ ∀τ ⊏ σ (D_σ <* D_τ) ("σ is a strict record among its prefixes"). P is Π¹₁ in S, uniformly; let R_σ be trees computable from (S, σ) with R_σ ∈ WF ⇔ P(σ).

(i) If P(σ) then σ ∈ Ctb, so A ∩ [σ] ⊆ Sc(A) by (CB). (ii) Every z ∈ Sc(A) has a prefix satisfying P: by (CB) some z↾m is in Ctb; for the least such m all proper prefixes τ have D_τ ∈ IF, so P(z↾m). (iii) Along any x ∈ ℕ^ℕ only finitely many prefixes satisfy P: if σ₁ ⊏ σ₂ both satisfy P then rk D_{σ₂} < rk D_{σ₁}.

blocks.label: (iv)
proof: If Sc(A) is finite then {σ : P(σ)} is finite: by (i) every such σ has A ∩ [σ] nonempty and included in
Sc(A), so σ is a prefix of one of finitely many points, and (iii) applies to each.

steps: By (i) and (ii), PK(A) = A ∖ ⋃{[σ] : P(σ)}.

Forward map. Let Γ_σ := U_{R_σ} be the tree of Section 2, step 3, built from R_σ: [Γ_σ] = {0^ℕ} if P(σ), and [Γ_σ] is a nonempty closed set without isolated points otherwise. Let S′ := {⟨⟩} ∪ {⟨0⟩⌢τ : τ ∈ S} ∪ {⟨1 + ⌜σ⌝⟩⌢τ : σ ∈ ℕ^{<ℕ}, τ ∈ Γ_σ}, A′ := [S′]. The pieces A′ ∩ [⟨j⟩] are clopen in A′, so Sc(A′) = {0⌢z : z ∈ Sc(A)} ∪ {(1 + ⌜σ⌝)⌢0^ℕ : P(σ)}.
By 3(iv): Sc(A′) is infinite iff Sc(A) is infinite.
Backward map. Let (n, (b_i, x_i)_i) ∈ ScList_ℕᴺ(A′).

proof: • List: (b′_i, x′_i) with b′_i := 1 iff b_i = 1 and x_i(0) = 0, and x′_i := x_i with the first digit removed.
Then {x′_i : b′_i = 1} = Sc(A).
• Kernel: say σ is *signalled at stage s* if some i < s has b_i = 1 and x_i(0) = 1 + ⌜σ⌝. Let
U := {τ ∈ S : no prefix σ ⊆ τ is signalled at stage |τ|}. U is a tree, computable from S and the list, and [U] = A ∖ ⋃{[σ] : P(σ)} = PK(A) by steps 5 and 4.
• Count: if n = 0 output 0 (step 6). If n = N + 1, search the list for N entries with b_i = 1 that are

pairwise distinct (distinctness of reals is semi-decidable; the search ends because Sc(A′) has exactly N elements, all listed); these are all the elements of Sc(A′); output 1 + the number of them with first digit 0. So (U, (output count, (b′_i, x′_i)_i)) ∈ CB_ℕᴺ(A).

items.dependencies: (CB), (EP), (SG); the Π¹₁ norm on WF and the fact that T <* T′ :⇔ T ∈ WF ∧ (T′ ∈ IF ∨ rk T < rk T′) is Π¹₁ (classical; directly: T <* T′ iff T ∈ WF and there is no map f : T′ → T with σ ⊏ τ ⇒ f(σ) ⊏ f(τ)); CMV Theorem 2.11(i),(ii).
items.concerns: finiteness of the pollution* (step 3(iv)). The signals needed to describe PK(A) are Π¹₁ facts "A ∩ [σ] is countable"; taken naively there are infinitely many true ones as soon as Sc(A) ≠ ∅, which would make ScCount(A′) infinite and lose ScCount(A). The record predicate P keeps finitely many per scattered point; that P is Π¹₁ uses that <* is Π¹₁ on *all* pairs of trees (not only on WF × WF). Nonemptiness in Ctb is needed (without it dead ends of S would give infinitely many signals) and is Π¹₁ only thanks to (EP)+(SG). (ii) The gadget "one point or perfect, according to a Π¹₁ condition" exists in Baire space only: in Cantor space |[B]| = 1 is Π⁰₂, and indeed ScList_{2^ℕ} <_W CB_{2^ℕ} (CMV Theorem 4.35); for trees the solution of CB contains the kernel as a set of nodes (negative information), and ScList_ℕᴺ <_W WF^ ≡_W CB (CMV Theorem 4.29, Proposition 4.34). So the argument does not prove too much. (iii) Edge cases: A = ∅ (U = S is a well-founded name of ∅, N = 0); Sc(A) infinite with finitely many records (n = 0 anyway since Sc(A′) ⊇ 0⌢Sc(A)). (iv) The reduction is Weihrauch, not claimed strong (the backward map uses S).

blocks.label: Proof
proof: Suppose ScCount_ℕᴺ × PK_ℕᴺ ≤_W ScList_ℕᴺ via Φ, Ψ.

steps: Let A₂ ⊆ 2^ℕ ⊆ ℕ^ℕ be the computable closed set A′ of Section 4, corollary 6. For every tree U on ℕ with [U] = PK(A₂), the Π¹₁-complete set W is Σ⁰₁ in U (apply corollary 6 to the binary tree U ∩ 2^{<ℕ}).

For a tree T let B_T := [U_T] as in Section 2, step 3: B_T = {0^ℕ} if T ∈ WF and B_T is perfect nonempty if T ∈ IF. So ScCount(B_T) = 2 if T ∈ WF and 1 if T ∈ IF. Let x_T := (B_T, A₂), S_T := Φ(x_T), A_T := [S_T].

For computable T, Sc(A_T) is infinite. Otherwise Sc(A_T) = {z_1, …, z_N} with all z_j hyperarithmetic (EP), and L := ((1, z_1), …, (1, z_N), (0, 0^ℕ), (0, 0^ℕ), …) gives a hyperarithmetic (N+1, L) ∈ ScList(A_T). Then Ψ(x_T, (N+1, L)) contains a hyperarithmetic name U of PK(A₂), and W would be Σ⁰₁ in a hyperarithmetic set, hence Δ¹₁: contradiction.
So for computable T the count of A_T is 0̄ and, for every L ∈ wScList(A_T), the first component of Ψ(x_T, (0, L)) is ScCount(B_T).

Let V_T := {σ : [σ] ∩ Sc(A_T) ≠ ∅}, Π¹₁ uniformly in an index of T (Section 1, step 2). Call a finite sequence φ = (b_i, σ_i)_{i<k} valid for T if b_i = 1 ⇒ σ_i ∈ V_T. The finite parts of the elements of wScList(A_T) are exactly the valid φ (for ⇐, choose y_i ∈ Sc(A_T) ∩ [σ_i] when b_i = 1 and append a list of Sc(A_T)).

Hence for the computable sequence (T_e) of Section 3 (Z = ∅): T_e ∈ IF ⇔ ∃φ valid for T_e such that Ψ(x_{T_e}, (0, φ)) outputs 1 as first component using only φ. (⇒: a finite part of any L. ⇐: φ extends to some L, on which the output must be ScCount(B_{T_e}); it is 1 only if T_e ∈ IF.) The right-hand side is Π¹₁ in e, but {e : T_e ∈ IF} is Σ¹₁-complete: contradiction. So ScCount_ℕᴺ × PK_ℕᴺ ≰_W ScList_ℕᴺ.
ScCount_ℕᴺ × PK_ℕᴺ ≤_W WF^{u*} × PK_ℕᴺ ≤_W C_ℕ ∗ PK_ℕᴺ, and ScList_ℕᴺ ≡_W CB_ℕᴺ (Section 12; for the facts as stated with from: sclist-baire, Section 12 is not needed).

blocks.label: Conventions
proof: Snapshot queried with cache/proofs/q.mjs. Convention of the database: an implication from A to B means B ≤ A; a separation from A to B means B ≰ A. All ideals below are Turing ideals (ω-models of RCA₀). "Classical" marks a textbook theorem named, not read in cache/fulltext. Nothing here depends on [@cintioli2026] or [@cintioli2026b].

Notation used throughout. A set G is *n-generic relative to Z* if for every Σ⁰ₙ(Z) set S of binary strings, G *meets* S (some initial segment of G is in S) or *avoids* S (some initial segment of G has no extension in S). An avoiding initial segment may always be taken as long as we wish. Σ⁰ₙ(W) ⊆ Σ⁰ₙ(Z) when W ≤_T Z, so n-generic relative to Z implies n-generic relative to W; Σ⁰₁(Z′) ⊆ Σ⁰₂(Z), so 2-generic relative to Z implies 1-generic relative to Z′ (and (n+1)-generic relative to Z implies n-generic relative to Z′).
Two lemmas are used by several sections.

proof.label: Lemma G (2-generics add no member to a Π⁰₁(Z′) class)
proof.text: Let G be 2-generic relative to Z, and let Q = [T] ⊆ ω^ω where T ⊆ ω^{<ω} is a Z′-computable tree. If some member of Q is computable in G ⊕ Z, then Q has a Z-computable member.
proof: 1. Let Φ^{G⊕Z} = a ∈ Q, with Φ a functional with the usual monotone use convention. Write Φ^{σ⊕Z} for the finite sequence ⟨Φ^{σ⊕Z}(0), …, Φ^{σ⊕Z}(m−1)⟩ where m is least with Φ^{σ⊕Z}(m) undefined in |σ| steps.

steps: Let A = {σ : ∃x ∀τ ⊇ σ Φ^{τ⊕Z}(x)↑} and B = {σ : Φ^{σ⊕Z} ∉ T}. A is Σ⁰₂(Z); B is Σ⁰₁(Z′), hence Σ⁰₂(Z). So A ∪ B is Σ⁰₂(Z).
G does not meet A (Φ^{G⊕Z} is total) and does not meet B (every initial segment of a is in T). So G avoids A ∪ B: there is σ₀ ≺ G no extension of which is in A ∪ B.
Define Z-computably τ₀ = σ₀ and τ_{i+1} = the first τ ⊇ τ_i found with Φ^{τ⊕Z}(i)↓. It exists because τ_i ⊇ σ₀ is not in A. Let ψ(i) = Φ^{τ_{i+1}⊕Z}(i).
ψ is total and Z-computable, and ψ↾n is an initial segment of Φ^{τ_n⊕Z}, which is in T because τ_n ∉ B and T is a tree. So ψ ∈ [T] = Q.

proof.label: Lemma D (2-generics add no dominating function)
proof.text: Let G be 2-generic relative to Z. Suppose that no Z-computable function eventually dominates every computable function. Then no function computable in G ⊕ Z eventually dominates every computable function.
proof: 1. Let f = Φ^{G⊕Z} be total. As in Lemma G (steps 2–3 with A alone), fix σ₀ ≺ G such that every ρ ⊇ σ₀ and every x have some τ ⊇ ρ with Φ^{τ⊕Z}(x)↓.

steps: For ρ ⊇ σ₀ and x let τ(ρ, x) be the first such τ found. Define the total Z-computable function g₁(x) = 1 + max{Φ^{τ(ρ,x)⊕Z}(x) : ρ ⊇ σ₀, |ρ| = |σ₀| + x}.
By hypothesis there is a computable g₀ with g₁(x) < g₀(x) for infinitely many x.

For each k let E_k = {τ ⊇ σ₀ : ∃x > k (g₁(x) < g₀(x) ∧ Φ^{τ⊕Z}(x)↓ < g₁(x))}. It is Σ⁰₁(Z). It is dense below σ₀: given ρ′ ⊇ σ₀, choose x > k with g₁(x) < g₀(x) and |σ₀| + x ≥ |ρ′|, extend ρ′ to ρ of length |σ₀| + x; then τ(ρ, x) ⊇ ρ′ and Φ^{τ(ρ,x)⊕Z}(x) ≤ g₁(x) − 1.

G is 1-generic relative to Z, and cannot avoid E_k (an avoiding initial segment can be taken ⊇ σ₀, contradicting density below σ₀). So G meets every E_k: for every k there is x > k with f(x) < g₁(x) < g₀(x). Hence f does not eventually dominate g₀.

proof.label: The generic ideal 𝓘_gen
proof: Let Z₀ = ∅ and Z_{i+1} = Z_i ⊕ G_i, where G_i is n-generic

relative to Z_i for every n (such G_i exists: meet or avoid the countably many arithmetical-in-Z_i sets of strings one after the other). Let 𝓘_gen = {X : ∃i X ≤_T Z_i}. It is a Turing ideal since Z_i ≤_T Z_{i+1}. By induction on i, using Lemma G (a Π⁰₁(∅′) class is a Π⁰₁(Z_i′) class) and Lemma D:
• (P1) every Π⁰₁(∅′) class Q ⊆ ω^ω with a member in 𝓘_gen has a computable member;
• (P2) no function in 𝓘_gen eventually dominates every computable function;
• (P3) Z_i′ ≡_T Z_i ⊕ ∅′ for every i, and every Π⁰₁(∅′) class with a member computable in
Z_i ⊕ ∅′ has a ∅′-computable member.

proof.label: Proof of (P3)
proof: If G is 1-generic relative to Z then (G ⊕ Z)′ ≤_T G ⊕ Z′: e ∈ (G ⊕ Z)′ iff G meets the Σ⁰₁(Z) set S_e = {σ : Φ_e^{σ⊕Z}(e)↓}, and e ∉ (G ⊕ Z)′ iff G avoids S_e; "G meets S_e" and "G avoids S_e" are both Σ⁰₁(G ⊕ Z′) and exactly one holds. So Z_{i+1}′ ≡_T G_i ⊕ Z_i′ ≡_T G_i ⊕ Z_i ⊕ ∅′ = Z_{i+1} ⊕ ∅′ by induction. For the second part, G_i is 3-generic relative to Z_i, hence 2-generic relative to Z_i′ ≡_T Z_i ⊕ ∅′; apply Lemma G with oracle Z_i ⊕ ∅′ in place of Z (a Π⁰₁(∅′) class is Π⁰₁((Z_i ⊕ ∅′)′)), and the induction hypothesis.

blocks.label: Proof
proof: Let 𝓘_gen be the ideal defined in the preliminaries, with properties (P1)–(P3).

steps: 𝓘_gen ⊨ (*). If Z ∈ 𝓘_gen then Z ≤_T Z_i for some i, and G_i ∈ 𝓘_gen is n-generic relative to Z_i, hence relative to Z, for every n. Apply section 2.

No DNC function. The DNC functions are the paths of the computable tree {σ ∈ ω^{<ω} : ∀e < |σ| ¬(φ_{e,|σ|}(e)↓ = σ(e))}, a Π⁰₁ class with no computable member. By (P1) it has no member in 𝓘_gen. So 𝓘_gen ⊭ DNR.

No SDNR. Let f(⟨e, n⟩) = φ_e(⟨e, n⟩) if this converges, and 0 otherwise; f is the limit of the computable approximation h(⟨e, n⟩, s) = φ_{e,s}(⟨e, n⟩) if converged, else 0, which changes at most once. Every total computable g = φ_e satisfies g(⟨e, 0⟩) = f(⟨e, 0⟩), so no computable function diagonalizes f. The class {g : ∀x g(x) ≠ f(x)} is the set of paths of the ∅′-computable tree {σ : ∀x < |σ| σ(x) ≠ f(x)}. By (P1) it has no member in 𝓘_gen. So the computable instance h has no solution in 𝓘_gen.

No SADS. Let L be the order of [@hirschfeldtshore2007], Theorem 2.1. The classes Q_asc = {a ∈ ω^ω : ∀i (a(i) < a(i+1) ∧ a(i) <_L a(i+1))} and Q_desc (with >_L) are Π⁰₁. A computable member of Q_asc has a computable range (it is increasing in ℕ), which is a computable suborder of type ω; similarly for Q_desc and ω*. So neither has a computable member, and by (P1) neither has a member in 𝓘_gen. proof.label: Lemma G (2-generics add no member to a Π⁰₁(Z′) class)
proof.text: Let G be 2-generic relative to Z, and let Q = [T] ⊆ ω^ω where T ⊆ ω^{<ω} is a Z′-computable tree. If some member of Q is computable in G ⊕ Z, then Q has a Z-computable member.
proof: 1. Let Φ^{G⊕Z} = a ∈ Q, with Φ a functional with the usual monotone use convention. Write Φ^{σ⊕Z} for the finite sequence ⟨Φ^{σ⊕Z}(0), …, Φ^{σ⊕Z}(m−1)⟩ where m is least with Φ^{σ⊕Z}(m) undefined in |σ| steps.

steps: Let A = {σ : ∃x ∀τ ⊇ σ Φ^{τ⊕Z}(x)↑} and B = {σ : Φ^{σ⊕Z} ∉ T}. A is Σ⁰₂(Z); B is Σ⁰₁(Z′), hence Σ⁰₂(Z). So A ∪ B is Σ⁰₂(Z).
G does not meet A (Φ^{G⊕Z} is total) and does not meet B (every initial segment of a is in T). So G avoids A ∪ B: there is σ₀ ≺ G no extension of which is in A ∪ B.
Define Z-computably τ₀ = σ₀ and τ_{i+1} = the first τ ⊇ τ_i found with Φ^{τ⊕Z}(i)↓. It exists because τ_i ⊇ σ₀ is not in A. Let ψ(i) = Φ^{τ_{i+1}⊕Z}(i).
ψ is total and Z-computable, and ψ↾n is an initial segment of Φ^{τ_n⊕Z}, which is in T because τ_n ∉ B and T is a tree. So ψ ∈ [T] = Q.

proof.text: Let G be 2-generic relative to Z. Suppose that no Z-computable function eventually dominates every computable function. Then no function computable in G ⊕ Z eventually dominates every computable function.

steps: (Bounded ideals fail (*).) Let 𝓘 ⊆ Δ⁰ₙ for some n ≥ 1, and suppose 𝓘 ⊨ (*). By section 2 some X ∈ 𝓘 is n-generic. S = {σ : ∃i < |σ| σ(i) ≠ X(i)} is Δ⁰ₙ, hence Σ⁰ₙ. X does not meet S. X does not avoid S: every σ ≺ X has the extension σ⌢(1 − X(|σ|)) ∈ S. Contradiction.

(w2ran not low, not Δ⁰₂.) If Y = lim_s Y_s is Δ⁰₂, then {X : ∀n∃s > n (X↾n = Y_s↾n)} = {Y} is a Π⁰₂ null class, so Y is not weakly 2-random. A solution Y to the instance ∅ with Y′ ≤_T ∅′ would be Δ⁰₂.

For each n, the sets {Y ⊇ σ : Φ^{Z⊕Y}(n) = i}, i = 0, 1, together have measure > (2/3)·2^{−|σ|}, so one of them has measure > (1/3)·2^{−|σ|}; let g(n) be the first i found with this property (a Z-computable search). If g(n) = φ_n(n), then all Y ⊇ σ with Φ^{Z⊕Y}(n) = g(n) are outside S, a set of measure > (1/3)·2^{−|σ|} inside [σ] ∖ S, which has measure < (1/3)·2^{−|σ|}: contradiction. The right-hand side is Σ⁰₁(Z): contradiction. So {Y : A is Σ⁰₁(Z ⊕ Y)} is null.

By induction from step 1 (applied to Z^{(k−1)} in place of Z), if Y is (k+1)-random relative to Z then (Y ⊕ Z)^{(k)} ≤_T Y ⊕ Z^{(k)}. proof.text: Let G be 2-generic relative to Z, and let Q = [T] ⊆ ω^ω where T ⊆ ω^{<ω} is a Z′-computable tree. If some member of Q is computable in G ⊕ Z, then Q has a Z-computable member.
proof: 1. Let Φ^{G⊕Z} = a ∈ Q, with Φ a functional with the usual monotone use convention. Write Φ^{σ⊕Z} for the finite sequence ⟨Φ^{σ⊕Z}(0), …, Φ^{σ⊕Z}(m−1)⟩ where m is least with Φ^{σ⊕Z}(m) undefined in |σ| steps.

steps: Let A = {σ : ∃x ∀τ ⊇ σ Φ^{τ⊕Z}(x)↑} and B = {σ : Φ^{σ⊕Z} ∉ T}. A is Σ⁰₂(Z); B is Σ⁰₁(Z′), hence Σ⁰₂(Z). So A ∪ B is Σ⁰₂(Z).
G does not meet A (Φ^{G⊕Z} is total) and does not meet B (every initial segment of a is in T). So G avoids A ∪ B: there is σ₀ ≺ G no extension of which is in A ∪ B.
Define Z-computably τ₀ = σ₀ and τ_{i+1} = the first τ ⊇ τ_i found with Φ^{τ⊕Z}(i)↓. It exists because τ_i ⊇ σ₀ is not in A. Let ψ(i) = Φ^{τ_{i+1}⊕Z}(i).
ψ is total and Z-computable, and ψ↾n is an initial segment of Φ^{τ_n⊕Z}, which is in T because τ_n ∉ B and T is a tree. So ψ ∈ [T] = Q.

proof.label: Lemma D (2-generics add no dominating function)
proof.text: Let G be 2-generic relative to Z. Suppose that no Z-computable function eventually dominates every computable function. Then no function computable in G ⊕ Z eventually dominates every computable function.

steps: For ρ ⊇ σ₀ and x let τ(ρ, x) be the first such τ found. Define the total Z-computable function g₁(x) = 1 + max{Φ^{τ(ρ,x)⊕Z}(x) : ρ ⊇ σ₀, |ρ| = |σ₀| + x}.
By hypothesis there is a computable g₀ with g₁(x) < g₀(x) for infinitely many x.

proof.label: Proof of (P3)
proof: If G is 1-generic relative to Z then (G ⊕ Z)′ ≤_T G ⊕ Z′: e ∈ (G ⊕ Z)′ iff G meets the Σ⁰₁(Z) set S_e = {σ : Φ_e^{σ⊕Z}(e)↓}, and e ∉ (G ⊕ Z)′ iff G avoids S_e; "G meets S_e" and "G avoids S_e" are both Σ⁰₁(G ⊕ Z′) and exactly one holds. steps: Let G be the graph of [@bienvenupateyshafer2017], Lemma 6.2; it is computable and bipartite, hence locally 2-colorable and without odd cycles.

Equivalence used. If two vertices of H are joined by an odd-length path P, the subgraph induced by the vertices of P has no 2-coloring giving both ends color 0; so H is not homogeneous. Q = {a ∈ ω^ω : a strictly increasing ∧ ∀i < j (a(i), a(j) are not joined by an odd-length path of G)} is a Π⁰₁ class ("joined by an odd-length path" is Σ⁰₁). blocks.label: Proof
proof: A. (Not conservative over BΣ⁰₂.) By section 1, RCA₀ + (*) ⊢ Π⁰₁G; by [@hirschfeldtshoreslaman2009], Theorem 4.3, RCA₀ + BΣ⁰₂ + (*) ⊢ IΣ⁰₂. IΣ⁰₂ (with set parameters) is a Π¹₁ sentence not provable in RCA₀ + BΣ⁰₂. B. (Conservative over IΣ⁰ₙ.) Fix n ≥ 1, a countable M ⊨ RCA₀ + IΣ⁰ₙ and an M-generic X. Formulas below are arithmetical, with parameters from |M| ∪ S_M and a set constant Ẋ, in strictly alternating prenex form ∃x₁∀x₂… θ or ∀x₁∃x₂… θ with θ bounded (adjacent like quantifiers are contracted by the pairing function, which RCA₀ allows without changing the class Σ⁰_k or Π⁰_k).

steps: Forcing. For σ ∈ 2^{<M} and a bounded formula θ, let b_θ be a term bounding the terms t of the atoms "t ∈ Ẋ" met in evaluating θ, and θ^σ the result of replacing "t ∈ Ẋ" by "σ(t) = 1". Define σ ⊩ θ iff |σ| ≥ b_θ ∧ θ^σ; σ ⊩ ∃xψ iff ∃x (σ ⊩ ψ(x)); σ ⊩ ∀xψ iff ∀x∀τ ⊇ σ (|τ| ≥ b_ψ → ψ^τ(x)) when ψ is bounded, and iff ∀x∀τ ⊇ σ ∃ρ ⊇ τ (ρ ⊩ ψ(x)) otherwise. By (external) induction on the formula: for a Σ⁰_k formula φ, "σ ⊩ φ" is a Σ⁰_k formula of M, and for a Π⁰_k formula a Π⁰_k formula (like quantifiers are merged by pairing; no collection is used). Forcing is monotone: σ ⊩ φ and τ ⊇ σ imply τ ⊩ φ.
Every initial segment X↾b (b ∈ |M|) is in 2^{<M}: X meets the dense set of strings of length ≥ b.
Truth lemma: (M, X) ⊨ φ iff ∃σ ≺ X (σ ⊩ φ), by induction on φ.

proof: • Bounded θ: both sides say θ^{X↾b_θ}.
• ∃xψ: immediate from the induction hypothesis.

• ∀xψ, ψ bounded. (⇐) For each x take τ = X↾max(|σ|, b_ψ). (⇒) D = {ρ : ρ ⊩ ∀xψ ∨ ∃x (|ρ| ≥ b_ψ ∧ ¬ψ^ρ(x))} is definable and dense (if ρ does not force ∀xψ, some τ ⊇ ρ is in the second part). X meets D at ρ; the second alternative would give (M, X) ⊨ ¬ψ(x); so ρ ⊩ ∀xψ.

• ∀xψ, ψ not bounded. (⇐) Let σ ≺ X force ∀xψ and fix x. D_x = {ρ : ρ ⊩ ψ(x) ∨ ∀π ⊇ ρ ¬(π ⊩ ψ(x))} is definable and dense; X meets it at ρ, and we may assume ρ ⊇ σ by monotonicity (both alternatives persist to extensions). The second alternative contradicts σ ⊩ ∀xψ (with τ = ρ). So ρ ⊩ ψ(x) and (M, X) ⊨ ψ(x) by induction. (⇒) D = {ρ : ρ ⊩ ∀xψ ∨ ∃x∀π ⊇ ρ ¬(π ⊩ ψ(x))} is definable and dense. X meets it at ρ. In the second case, with witness x: (M, X) ⊨ ψ(x), so by induction some σ ≺ X forces ψ(x), and the longer of σ, ρ is an extension of ρ forcing ψ(x): contradiction. So ρ ⊩ ∀xψ.

steps: Σ⁰ₙ induction in (|M|, S_M ∪ {X}). Let φ(m) be Σ⁰ₙ and suppose (M, X) ⊨ φ(0) ∧ ∀m(φ(m) → φ(m+1)) ∧ ¬φ(a). a. E₁ = {ρ : ∃m (ρ ⊩ φ(m) ∧ ∀π ⊇ ρ ¬(π ⊩ φ(m+1)))}, and E = E₁ ∪ {ρ : no extension of ρ is in E₁}. E is definable and dense; X meets it at ρ₀. If ρ₀ ∈ E₁ with witness m, then (M, X) ⊨ φ(m) by step 3, and (M, X) ⊭ φ(m+1) (otherwise some σ ≺ X forces φ(m+1), and the longer of σ, ρ₀ is an extension of ρ₀ forcing it): this contradicts the hypothesis. So no extension of ρ₀ is in E₁. b. F = {ρ : ρ ⊩ φ(a) ∨ ∀π ⊇ ρ ¬(π ⊩ φ(a))} is definable and dense; X meets it at ρ₁, and ρ₁ ⊩ φ(a) is impossible by step 3. Let σ₁ be the longer of ρ₀, ρ₁: σ₁ ≺ X, σ₁ ⊇ ρ₀, and no extension of σ₁ forces φ(a). c. In M let ψ̂(m) :≡ ∃τ ⊇ σ₁ (τ ⊩ φ(m)), a Σ⁰ₙ formula by step 1. ψ̂(0) holds: some σ ≺ X forces φ(0) by step 3, and the longer of σ, σ₁ extends σ₁ and forces φ(0). ψ̂(a) fails by b. By Σ⁰ₙ induction in M there is m < a with ψ̂(m) ∧ ¬ψ̂(m+1): some τ ⊇ σ₁ forces φ(m) and no extension of σ₁, a fortiori of τ, forces φ(m+1). Then τ ∈ E₁ and τ ⊇ ρ₀: contradiction with a.

By the Σ⁰ₙ analogue of [@brownsimpson1993], Lemma 6.1, M[X] = (|M|, Δ⁰₁-Def(S_M ∪ {X})) ⊨ RCA₀ + IΣ⁰ₙ; M is a submodel with the same first-order part, and X ∈ S_{M[X]} meets every M-definable dense set.

Iterate: M₀ = M, M_{i+1} = M_i[X_i] with X_i M_i-generic (M_i is countable), M_ω = (|M|, ⋃S_{M_i}). An arithmetical formula with parameters in M_i has the same truth value in M_i and in M_ω (same first-order part). So M_ω ⊨ RCA₀ + IΣ⁰ₙ. M_ω ⊨ (*): if φ(m, τ) has its parameters in M_i and ∀m∀σ∃τ ⊇ σ φ(m, τ) holds, then for every m ∈ |M| the set {τ : φ(m, τ)} is M_i-definable and dense, so X_i meets it: ∀m∃k φ(m, X_i[k]).
If RCA₀ + IΣ⁰ₙ ⊬ ∀Y θ(Y) with θ arithmetical, take a countable M ⊨ RCA₀ + IΣ⁰ₙ + ¬θ(Y) for some Y ∈ S_M; then M_ω ⊨ RCA₀ + IΣ⁰ₙ + (*) + ¬θ(Y). So RCA₀ + IΣ⁰ₙ + (*) ⊬ ∀Y θ(Y).

proof: 1. Let Φ^{G⊕Z} = a ∈ Q, with Φ a functional with the usual monotone use convention. Write Φ^{σ⊕Z} for the finite sequence ⟨Φ^{σ⊕Z}(0), …, Φ^{σ⊕Z}(m−1)⟩ where m is least with Φ^{σ⊕Z}(m) undefined in |σ| steps.

steps: Let A = {σ : ∃x ∀τ ⊇ σ Φ^{τ⊕Z}(x)↑} and B = {σ : Φ^{σ⊕Z} ∉ T}. A is Σ⁰₂(Z); B is Σ⁰₁(Z′), hence Σ⁰₂(Z). So A ∪ B is Σ⁰₂(Z).
G does not meet A (Φ^{G⊕Z} is total) and does not meet B (every initial segment of a is in T). So G avoids A ∪ B: there is σ₀ ≺ G no extension of which is in A ∪ B.
Define Z-computably τ₀ = σ₀ and τ_{i+1} = the first τ ⊇ τ_i found with Φ^{τ⊕Z}(i)↓. It exists because τ_i ⊇ σ₀ is not in A. Let ψ(i) = Φ^{τ_{i+1}⊕Z}(i).
ψ is total and Z-computable, and ψ↾n is an initial segment of Φ^{τ_n⊕Z}, which is in T because τ_n ∉ B and T is a tree. So ψ ∈ [T] = Q.

proof.label: Lemma D (2-generics add no dominating function)
proof.text: Let G be 2-generic relative to Z. Suppose that no Z-computable function eventually dominates every computable function. Then no function computable in G ⊕ Z eventually dominates every computable function.
proof: 1. Let f = Φ^{G⊕Z} be total. As in Lemma G (steps 2–3 with A alone), fix σ₀ ≺ G such that every ρ ⊇ σ₀ and every x have some τ ⊇ ρ with Φ^{τ⊕Z}(x)↓.

steps: For ρ ⊇ σ₀ and x let τ(ρ, x) be the first such τ found. Define the total Z-computable function g₁(x) = 1 + max{Φ^{τ(ρ,x)⊕Z}(x) : ρ ⊇ σ₀, |ρ| = |σ₀| + x}.

For each k let E_k = {τ ⊇ σ₀ : ∃x > k (g₁(x) < g₀(x) ∧ Φ^{τ⊕Z}(x)↓ < g₁(x))}. It is Σ⁰₁(Z). It is dense below σ₀: given ρ′ ⊇ σ₀, choose x > k with g₁(x) < g₀(x) and |σ₀| + x ≥ |ρ′|, extend ρ′ to ρ of length |σ₀| + x; then τ(ρ, x) ⊇ ρ′ and Φ^{τ(ρ,x)⊕Z}(x) ≤ g₁(x) − 1.

proof.label: The generic ideal 𝓘_gen
proof: Let Z₀ = ∅ and Z_{i+1} = Z_i ⊕ G_i, where G_i is n-generic

relative to Z_i for every n (such G_i exists: meet or avoid the countably many arithmetical-in-Z_i sets of strings one after the other). Let 𝓘_gen = {X : ∃i X ≤_T Z_i}. It is a Turing ideal since Z_i ≤_T Z_{i+1}. By induction on i, using Lemma G (a Π⁰₁(∅′) class is a Π⁰₁(Z_i′) class) and Lemma D:
• (P1) every Π⁰₁(∅′) class Q ⊆ ω^ω with a member in 𝓘_gen has a computable member;

• (P3) Z_i′ ≡_T Z_i ⊕ ∅′ for every i, and every Π⁰₁(∅′) class with a member computable in

proof.label: Proof of (P3)
proof: If G is 1-generic relative to Z then (G ⊕ Z)′ ≤_T G ⊕ Z′: e ∈ (G ⊕ Z)′ iff G meets the Σ⁰₁(Z) set S_e = {σ : Φ_e^{σ⊕Z}(e)↓}, and e ∉ (G ⊕ Z)′ iff G avoids S_e; "G meets S_e" and "G avoids S_e" are both Σ⁰₁(G ⊕ Z′) and exactly one holds. steps: Common argument. Take the computable KPT-instance r = ∅. Suppose KPT ≤_c Q, and let X̂ be the computable Q-instance assigned to r. If X̂ has a solution Ŷ of minimal degree, or a computable one, then every set computable in r ⊕ Ŷ is computable or Turing equivalent to Ŷ, so no two sets computable in r ⊕ Ŷ are incomparable: r ⊕ Ŷ computes no KPT-solution. So it suffices to show that every computable Q-instance has a solution which is computable or of minimal degree.

Q = HYP. Let a < 0′ be minimal; it is hyperimmune ([@millermartin1968], Section 3), so some function q of degree ≤ a, hence of degree a, is not dominated by any computable function; modifying finitely many values does not matter, so for every computable r̂ there is n with r̂(n) < q(n). For a computable instance p, the functions computable in p are the computable functions, so q ∈ HYP(p).

Q = COH. Let a be a high minimal degree. By Jockusch's theorem a contains a cohesive set C. C is cohesive for every uniformly computable sequence of sets, i.e. a solution to every computable COH-instance, and it has minimal degree.

Q = CR. Let A have high minimal degree. By Martin's theorem A is high relative to ∅ in the sense of [@niesshafer2020], so A computes a computably random set R; R is not computable, so R ≡_T A has minimal degree. A computable instance Z has the same computably random sets as ∅ (the supermartingales computable in Z are the computable ones), so R is a solution to every computable instance.

items.dependencies: [@millermartin1968], Section 3: "Sacks shows that there is a minimal degree < 0′, which by Theorem 1.2 cannot be hyperimmune-free", with Corollary 1.1 there (a degree is hyperimmune iff some function of degree ≤ a is not dominated by a recursive function) — read in the text (OCR). [@jockuschstephan1993], p. 519: "all high degrees are cohesive [Jockusch 1973, Corollary 2]". [@niesshafer2020], proof of Proposition 7.2, item (i): if A is high relative to B (a function f ≤_T A eventually dominates every g ≤_T B) then A ⊕ B computes a set computably random relative to B. The existence of a high minimal degree (classical: Cooper 1973, Minimal degrees and the jump operator; not read in cache/fulltext), and Martin's theorem that a high set computes a function dominating all computable functions (classical).
items.concerns: the reduction ≤_c lets the forward functional choose the Q-instance, but from the computable r it can only produce a computable instance, and in each case one fixed solution works for all computable instances. Step 1 uses that "p |_T q with ⟨p, q⟩ computable in Ŷ" needs two incomparable degrees below deg(Ŷ). The citation of Cooper's theorem is from memory (standard); steps 2 uses only texts read. The result does not transfer to ω-models, where further solutions are available.

steps: Construction. Z₀ = ∅. At even stages, Z_{i+1} = Z_i ⊕ G where G is n-generic relative to Z_i for every n. At odd stages, take the next pair ⟨k, e⟩ (k ≤ i) in a fixed enumeration in which every pair occurs; if Φ_e^{Z_k} is an infinite binary tree, let X be a path through it with (X ⊕ Z_i)′ ≤_T Z_i′ and Z_{i+1} = Z_i ⊕ X; otherwise Z_{i+1} = Z_i. Let 𝓘 = {Y : ∃i Y ≤_T Z_i}.

𝓘 ⊨ WKL (every infinite binary tree in 𝓘 is Φ_e^{Z_k} for some ⟨k, e⟩ and gets a path) and 𝓘 ⊨ (*) (section 2: for Z ≤_T Z_i take an even stage j ≥ i; its G is n-generic relative to Z_j, hence relative to Z).

Invariant. Let Q be a Π⁰₁(∅′) class in ω^ω with no ∅′-computable member. Then no Z_i′ computes a member of Q. Base: Z₀′ = ∅′. Odd stages: Z_{i+1}′ ≤_T Z_i′. Even stages: G is 1-generic relative to Z_i, so Z_{i+1}′ ≤_T G ⊕ Z_i′ (proof of (P3) in the preliminaries); G is 3-generic relative to Z_i, hence 2-generic relative to W = Z_i′; Q is a Π⁰₁(W′) class since ∅′ ≤_T W; by Lemma G with oracle W, a member of Q computable in G ⊕ W would give a W-computable member, contradicting the induction hypothesis.
Take Q = {h : ∀e ¬(Φ_e^{∅′}(e)↓ = h(e))}, the set of paths of the ∅′-computable tree {σ : ∀e < |σ| ¬(Φ_{e,|σ|}^{∅′}(e)↓ = σ(e))}; it has no ∅′-computable member.

items.dependencies: the low basis theorem relativized (classical, Jockusch–Soare 1972): every infinite Z-computable binary tree has a path X with (X ⊕ Z)′ ≤_T Z′. [@jockuschstephan1993], Theorem 2.1 (⇒). Lemma G and section 2.
items.concerns: the invariant is about the jumps Z_i′, not about Z_i ⊕ ∅′: the low basis theorem keeps the jump inside Z_i′ but the path itself is only computable from Z_i′, which is why the invariant of section 4 (P1) cannot be used here (WKL adds members to Π⁰₁ classes without computable members) and the result is limited to principles that code into the jump. The model necessarily contains DNC functions, 1-randoms and Schnorr randoms. Whether WKL₀⁺ proves SADS, 2-SDNR or W2R on ω-models is not decided here (for the particular function f of section 4, step 3, every set of PA degree computes an f-diagonalizing function, so another instance would be needed).

The quantifiers ∃ρ∃m are bounded by σ, so (D_i) is uniformly Π⁰₁.
Each D_i is dense: given τ, let ρ ⊇ τ with |ρ| ≥ i, and take m ≥ g(|ρ|) so large that g_s(|ρ|) = g(|ρ|) for all s ≥ m; then ρ⌢1^m⌢0 ∈ D_i extends τ.

Let G meet every D_i. For each i there are ρ_i, m_i with |ρ_i| ≥ i, ρ_i⌢1^{m_i}⌢0 ≺ G and g(|ρ_i|) ≤ m_i. In particular G has infinitely many zeros, so f(n) = the number of consecutive ones of G starting at position n is total and f ≤_T G. f(|ρ_i|) = m_i ≥ g(|ρ_i|), and |ρ_i| ≥ i: so f(n) ≥ g(n) for infinitely many n.
Hence if g(n) > f(n) for almost all n, for every function f ∈ 𝓘, the computable instance (D_i) of Π⁰₁G has no solution in 𝓘.

(Uniform steps.) (L1) There are functionals Γ, Δ such that for every Z, G = Γ^{Z′} is 1-generic relative to Z and (Z ⊕ G)′ = Δ^{Z′}: build G = ⋃σ_n; at step 2e, if some τ ⊇ σ_{2e} is in the e-th Σ⁰₁(Z) set of strings (a Σ⁰₁(Z) question, answered by Z′) let σ_{2e+1} be the first such τ found, else σ_{2e+1} = σ_{2e}⌢0; at step 2e+1, if some τ ⊇ σ_{2e+1} has Φ_e^{Z⊕τ}(e)↓ let σ_{2e+2} be the first one found and Δ^{Z′}(e) = 1, else σ_{2e+2} = σ_{2e+1}⌢0 and Δ^{Z′}(e) = 0. (L2) There are functionals Γ′, Δ′ such that for every Z, X = Γ′^{Z′} is a {0,1}-valued DNC function relative to Z and (Z ⊕ X)′ = Δ′^{Z′}: this is the proof of the low basis theorem for the nonempty Π⁰₁(Z) class P₀ = {X ∈ 2^ω : ∀e ¬(Φ_e^Z(e)↓ = X(e))}: at step 2e let P_{2e+1} = P_{2e} ∩ {X : Φ_e^{Z⊕X}(e)↑} if this Π⁰₁(Z) class is nonempty (emptiness is Σ⁰₁(Z)), and then Δ′(e) = 0, else P_{2e+1} = P_{2e} and Δ′(e) = 1; at step 2e+1 let P_{2e+2} = P_{2e+1} ∩ {X : X(e) = b} for the least b making it nonempty. X is the common element.

(The ideal.) Let Z₀ = ∅, Z_{2i+1} = Z_{2i} ⊕ Γ^{Z_{2i}′}, Z_{2i+2} = Z_{2i+1} ⊕ Γ′^{Z_{2i+1}′}. By induction with L1, L2, an index of Z_i′ as a ∅′-computable set is obtained computably from i; so the relation "Φ_e^{Z_i}(x)↓" and the values Φ_e^{Z_i}(x) are ∅′-computable uniformly in e, i, x. Let g(x) = 1 + max{Φ_e^{Z_i}(x) : e, i ≤ x, Φ_e^{Z_i}(x)↓}. Then g ≤_T ∅′ and g(x) > f(x) for all x ≥ max(e, i) whenever f = Φ_e^{Z_i} is total.

𝓘 = {Y : ∃i Y ≤_T Z_i} satisfies 1-GEN (for Y ≤_T Z_i take an even stage 2j ≥ i: its generic is 1-generic relative to Z_{2j}, hence to Y) and WKL (an infinite binary tree T ≤_T Z_i has a path computable in Z_{2j+2} for 2j+1 ≥ i), hence 1-RAN. Every function of 𝓘 is eventually dominated by g. By Lemma E, 𝓘 ⊭ Π⁰₁G.

blocks.label: Conventions
proof: Snapshot queried with cache/proofs/q.mjs. Convention of the database: an implication from A to B means B ≤ A; a separation from A to B means B ≰ A. All ideals below are Turing ideals (ω-models of RCA₀). "Classical" marks a textbook theorem named, not read in cache/fulltext. Nothing here depends on [@cintioli2026] or [@cintioli2026b].

Notation used throughout. A set G is *n-generic relative to Z* if for every Σ⁰ₙ(Z) set S of binary strings, G *meets* S (some initial segment of G is in S) or *avoids* S (some initial segment of G has no extension in S). An avoiding initial segment may always be taken as long as we wish. Σ⁰ₙ(W) ⊆ Σ⁰ₙ(Z) when W ≤_T Z, so n-generic relative to Z implies n-generic relative to W; Σ⁰₁(Z′) ⊆ Σ⁰₂(Z), so 2-generic relative to Z implies 1-generic relative to Z′ (and (n+1)-generic relative to Z implies n-generic relative to Z′).
Two lemmas are used by several sections.

proof.label: Lemma G (2-generics add no member to a Π⁰₁(Z′) class)
proof.text: Let G be 2-generic relative to Z, and let Q = [T] ⊆ ω^ω where T ⊆ ω^{<ω} is a Z′-computable tree. If some member of Q is computable in G ⊕ Z, then Q has a Z-computable member.
proof: 1. Let Φ^{G⊕Z} = a ∈ Q, with Φ a functional with the usual monotone use convention. Write Φ^{σ⊕Z} for the finite sequence ⟨Φ^{σ⊕Z}(0), …, Φ^{σ⊕Z}(m−1)⟩ where m is least with Φ^{σ⊕Z}(m) undefined in |σ| steps.

steps: Let A = {σ : ∃x ∀τ ⊇ σ Φ^{τ⊕Z}(x)↑} and B = {σ : Φ^{σ⊕Z} ∉ T}. A is Σ⁰₂(Z); B is Σ⁰₁(Z′), hence Σ⁰₂(Z). So A ∪ B is Σ⁰₂(Z).
G does not meet A (Φ^{G⊕Z} is total) and does not meet B (every initial segment of a is in T). So G avoids A ∪ B: there is σ₀ ≺ G no extension of which is in A ∪ B.
Define Z-computably τ₀ = σ₀ and τ_{i+1} = the first τ ⊇ τ_i found with Φ^{τ⊕Z}(i)↓. It exists because τ_i ⊇ σ₀ is not in A. Let ψ(i) = Φ^{τ_{i+1}⊕Z}(i).
ψ is total and Z-computable, and ψ↾n is an initial segment of Φ^{τ_n⊕Z}, which is in T because τ_n ∉ B and T is a tree. So ψ ∈ [T] = Q.

proof.label: Lemma D (2-generics add no dominating function)
proof.text: Let G be 2-generic relative to Z. Suppose that no Z-computable function eventually dominates every computable function. Then no function computable in G ⊕ Z eventually dominates every computable function.
proof: 1. Let f = Φ^{G⊕Z} be total. As in Lemma G (steps 2–3 with A alone), fix σ₀ ≺ G such that every ρ ⊇ σ₀ and every x have some τ ⊇ ρ with Φ^{τ⊕Z}(x)↓.

steps: For ρ ⊇ σ₀ and x let τ(ρ, x) be the first such τ found. Define the total Z-computable function g₁(x) = 1 + max{Φ^{τ(ρ,x)⊕Z}(x) : ρ ⊇ σ₀, |ρ| = |σ₀| + x}.
By hypothesis there is a computable g₀ with g₁(x) < g₀(x) for infinitely many x.

For each k let E_k = {τ ⊇ σ₀ : ∃x > k (g₁(x) < g₀(x) ∧ Φ^{τ⊕Z}(x)↓ < g₁(x))}. It is Σ⁰₁(Z). It is dense below σ₀: given ρ′ ⊇ σ₀, choose x > k with g₁(x) < g₀(x) and |σ₀| + x ≥ |ρ′|, extend ρ′ to ρ of length |σ₀| + x; then τ(ρ, x) ⊇ ρ′ and Φ^{τ(ρ,x)⊕Z}(x) ≤ g₁(x) − 1.

G is 1-generic relative to Z, and cannot avoid E_k (an avoiding initial segment can be taken ⊇ σ₀, contradicting density below σ₀). So G meets every E_k: for every k there is x > k with f(x) < g₁(x) < g₀(x). Hence f does not eventually dominate g₀.

proof.label: The generic ideal 𝓘_gen
proof: Let Z₀ = ∅ and Z_{i+1} = Z_i ⊕ G_i, where G_i is n-generic

relative to Z_i for every n (such G_i exists: meet or avoid the countably many arithmetical-in-Z_i sets of strings one after the other). Let 𝓘_gen = {X : ∃i X ≤_T Z_i}. It is a Turing ideal since Z_i ≤_T Z_{i+1}. By induction on i, using Lemma G (a Π⁰₁(∅′) class is a Π⁰₁(Z_i′) class) and Lemma D:
• (P1) every Π⁰₁(∅′) class Q ⊆ ω^ω with a member in 𝓘_gen has a computable member;
• (P2) no function in 𝓘_gen eventually dominates every computable function;
• (P3) Z_i′ ≡_T Z_i ⊕ ∅′ for every i, and every Π⁰₁(∅′) class with a member computable in
Z_i ⊕ ∅′ has a ∅′-computable member.

proof.label: Proof of (P3)
proof: If G is 1-generic relative to Z then (G ⊕ Z)′ ≤_T G ⊕ Z′: e ∈ (G ⊕ Z)′ iff G meets the Σ⁰₁(Z) set S_e = {σ : Φ_e^{σ⊕Z}(e)↓}, and e ∉ (G ⊕ Z)′ iff G avoids S_e; "G meets S_e" and "G avoids S_e" are both Σ⁰₁(G ⊕ Z′) and exactly one holds. So Z_{i+1}′ ≡_T G_i ⊕ Z_i′ ≡_T G_i ⊕ Z_i ⊕ ∅′ = Z_{i+1} ⊕ ∅′ by induction. For the second part, G_i is 3-generic relative to Z_i, hence 2-generic relative to Z_i′ ≡_T Z_i ⊕ ∅′; apply Lemma G with oracle Z_i ⊕ ∅′ in place of Z (a Π⁰₁(∅′) class is Π⁰₁((Z_i ⊕ ∅′)′)), and the induction hypothesis.

blocks.label: Proof

steps: A. Let A ≤_T ∅′ be 1-generic. Its complement is 1-generic too (complementation is a computable bijection of strings preserving c.e. sets). A 1-generic set B is hyperimmune: B is infinite, and for a computable h and k the c.e. set of strings w⌢0^{h(|w|)+1} with |w| > k is dense, so p_B(n) > h(n) for some n > k (as in section 12, step 3). So A and its complement Ā are hyperimmune.

Construction. Z₀ = ∅. Even stages: Z_{i+1} = Z_i ⊕ G with G n-generic relative to Z_i for every n. Odd stages: for the next pair ⟨k, e⟩ with Φ_e^{Z_k} an infinite binary tree (k ≤ i), Z_{i+1} = Z_i ⊕ X where X is a path such that every function computable in X ⊕ Z_i is majorized by a Z_i-computable function. 𝓘 = {Y : ∃i Y ≤_T Z_i} ⊨ WKL + (*) as in section 20, step 2.
Invariant: A and Ā are Z_i-hyperimmune for every i. Let B be A or Ā.

proof: • Odd stage: if f ≤_T X ⊕ Z_i, then f ≤ h pointwise for some h ≤_T Z_i; h(x) < p_B(x) for infinitely many x; so f does not eventually dominate p_B.

• Even stage: let f = Φ^{G⊕Z} be total (Z = Z_i). As in Lemma D, steps 1–2, there are σ₀ ≺ G forcing totality and a Z-computable g₁ with: for every ρ′ ⊇ σ₀ and every x with |σ₀| + x ≥ |ρ′| some τ ⊇ ρ′ has Φ^{τ⊕Z}(x)↓ < g₁(x). Since B is Z-hyperimmune, g₁(x) < p_B(x) for infinitely many x. For each k the set E_k = {τ ⊇ σ₀ : ∃x > k (g₁(x) < p_B(x) ∧ Φ^{τ⊕Z}(x)↓ < g₁(x))} is Σ⁰₁(Z ⊕ B) and dense below σ₀. Since B ≤_T ∅′ ≤_T Z′, E_k is Σ⁰₁(Z′), hence Σ⁰₂(Z), and G (2-generic relative to Z) meets or avoids it; it cannot avoid it. So f(x) < g₁(x) < p_B(x) for infinitely many x.

steps: No member of 𝓘 is an infinite subset S of B: p_S ≥ p_B pointwise and S ≤_T Z_i would contradict the invariant.

Let A_s be a computable approximation of A and f(x, y) = A_y(x) for x < y: a computable stable coloring. An infinite limit-homogeneous set is an infinite subset of A or of Ā. By step 4 there is none in 𝓘. So 𝓘 ⊭ D²₂.

𝓘 ⊨ W2R: for Z ∈ 𝓘, Z ≤_T Z_i with i odd-stage index, the tree of a Π⁰₁(Z_i) class of sets 1-random relative to Z_i gets at some odd stage j ≥ i a path R all of whose joins R ⊕ Z_j compute only functions majorized by Z_j-computable functions; R is 1-random relative to Z_i but the argument of section 8, step 3 needs randomness relative to Z_j: take instead, at that stage, the tree Φ_e^{Z_k} with k = j (a Π⁰₁(Z_j) class of sets 1-random relative to Z_j; the enumeration of pairs can be arranged so that for every j such a pair ⟨j, e⟩ is treated at a stage whose current set is Z_j itself, for instance by treating at stage 2j+1 first this tree and at later stages the others). Then R is 1-random relative to Z_j and R ⊕ Z_j is hyperimmune-free relative to Z_j, so R is weakly 2-random relative to Z_j by the relativized argument of section 8, step 3, hence relative to Z.

items.dependencies: the hyperimmune-free basis theorem relativized (Jockusch–Soare 1972, Theorem 2.4, in the form used in [@brownsimpson1993], Lemma 6.11): every infinite Z-computable binary tree has a path X such that every function computable in X ⊕ Z is majorized by a Z-computable function. Existence of a 1-generic set A ≤_T ∅′ (classical). Sections 2 and 8.
items.concerns: the invariant uses two different mechanisms: at WKL steps, hyperimmune-freeness relative to the previous set; at generic steps, genericity relative to Z ⊕ B, which holds because B is Δ⁰₂ and G is 2-generic relative to Z. A low basis step (as in section 20) would not preserve the hyperimmunity of A, and the model of section 20 is a different one: the two results are not obtained in the same ideal. Step 6 is a remark and is not needed for the fact; its only delicate point (randomness relative to the current set) is handled by fixing the order of the stages. Whether WKL₀⁺ proves SADS on ω-models is left open: it would follow from the same invariant given a computable linear order of type ω + ω* whose two parts are hyperimmune, which I did not construct.

proof: Conventions used in every proof below.

• A name of a co-c.e. closed subset A of N (or of {0..k-1}) is a p ∈ N^N with p(i) = 0 ("nothing") or p(i) = m+1 ("m is removed"); A is the set of numbers never removed.

• "K(σ, c) = v" for a finite string σ means that the (continuous) functional K has already produced the output v after reading only σ and c; then K(x, c) = v for every x extending σ. All outputs for which this is used are natural numbers or finite tuples of bits.
• ≤cW (continuous Weihrauch reducibility) is used for the separations whenever the argument only uses continuity; a separation over cW gives the ones over W and sW.

• f ⋆ g is the compositional product: f ⋆ g ≡W max{f0 ∘ g0 : f0 ≤W f, g0 ≤W g} ([@brattkagherardipauly2021], Theorem 5.2 and Proposition 5.4; [@brattkapauly2018], Corollary 3.7), and dom(f0 ∘ g0) = {x ∈ dom(g0) : g0(x) ⊆ dom(f0)} ([@brattkagherardipauly2021], Definition 1.2).

steps: TC_N has codomain N. If TC_N ≤W WKL′ then TC_N ≤W ¹(WKL′) ≡W K′_N.
K′_N ≡sW BWT_N ≤W RT¹_N: a bounded sequence of numbers is a colouring of N with finitely many colours (number not given), and the colour of an infinite homogeneous set is a cluster point.
So TC_N ≤W RT¹_N, contradicting Proposition 7.35.

blocks.label: Proof of the separation
proof: Let BWT_3 be the auxiliary problem: given x ∈ 3^N, find c ∈ I(x) := {c < 3 : c occurs infinitely often in x}.

steps: BWT_3 ≤sW C_3′. Given x, let p_s(⟨c, k⟩) = c + 1 ("remove c") if c does not occur in x at any position in [k, s), and 0 otherwise. For fixed (c, k), p_s(⟨c, k⟩) is eventually constant, so (p_s)_s converges to some p; p removes c iff c does not occur after some k iff c ∉ I(x). So p is a name of I(x) ≠ ∅ and C_3′((p_s)_s) = I(x).

Suppose BWT_3 ≤W C_N ⋆ LPO′. Then there are g0 ≤W LPO′ via (H_g, K_g), f0 ≤W C_N via (H_f, K_f) and (H, K) reducing BWT_3 to f0 ∘ g0. For x ∈ 3^N: H_g(H(x)) is a sequence converging to some q(x) ∈ 2^N; let b(x) = LPO(q(x)) and D_i = {x : b(x) = i}. Since the sequence converges, q(x) = 0^ω iff for all k and s there is t ≥ s with H_g(H(x))(t)(k) = 0; so D_1 is a G_δ subset of 3^N and D_0 = 3^N \ D_1 is F_σ.

For x ∈ D_i, y = K_g(H(x), i) is a name of an element of g0(H(x)) ⊆ dom(f0), H_f(y) is a name of a nonempty A(x) ⊆ N, and for n ∈ A(x), s_{i,n}(x) := K(x, K_f(y, n)) ∈ I(x). All these maps are continuous on D_i. Hence S_{i,n} = {x ∈ D_i : n ∈ A(x)} is relatively closed in D_i, D_i = ∪_n S_{i,n}, and s_{i,n} is a continuous selector (a continuous map into {0,1,2} with s(x) ∈ I(x)) on S_{i,n}.
Write D_0 = ∪_m C_m with C_m closed in 3^N. Each S_{0,n} ∩ C_m is closed in 3^N. So D_0 is a countable union of closed sets P_j ⊆ 3^N, each carrying a continuous selector.
Lemma. If a ≠ b are colours and Z = τ{a,b}^N, there is no continuous selector on Z. Proof: s(τ a^ω) = a, already on a prefix τ a^m; but τ a^m b^ω ∈ Z has I = {b}.
Case D_1 meager. Then D_0 is comeager, so by the Baire category theorem some P_j is not nowhere dense: it contains a cone [τ] ⊇ τ{0,1}^N, contradicting the lemma.

Case D_1 non-meager. D_1 has the Baire property, so it is comeager in some cone [τ]; D_1 ∩ [τ] is a nonempty G_δ, hence a Polish space, covered by the relatively closed sets S_{1,n} ∩ [τ]. By the Baire category theorem some S_{1,n} contains D_1 ∩ [τ′] ≠ ∅ for some τ′ ⊇ τ. Take x* ∈ D_1 ∩ [τ′]; s_{1,n}(x*) = c is determined by a prefix τ″ ⊇ τ′ of x*, so c ∈ I(x) for all x ∈ D_1 ∩ [τ″].

Let a, b be the two colours ≠ c and Z = τ″{a,b}^N. No x ∈ Z has c ∈ I(x), so Z ∩ D_1 = ∅ and Z ⊆ D_0 = ∪_j P_j. Z is a compact space homeomorphic to 2^N; by the Baire category theorem some P_j ∩ Z contains a relatively open set ρ{a,b}^N, on which P_j's selector is continuous: contradiction with the lemma.
So BWT_3 ≰W C_N ⋆ LPO′, hence C_3′ ≰W C_N ⋆ LPO′ ≡W C_N ⋆ TC_N (Corollary 8.10).

The direction of Corollary 8.10 that is needed, C_N ⋆ TC_N ≤W C_N ⋆ LPO′, can be checked directly: for an enumeration e of B let p_s(n) = 0 if e has enumerated n before stage s and 1 otherwise; (p_s)_s converges to 1 − χ_B, so LPO′((p_s)_s) = 1 iff B = N; if it is 1 output 0, otherwise apply C_N to e. So TC_N ≤W C_N ⋆ LPO′, and C_N ⋆ TC_N ≤W C_N ⋆ C_N ⋆ LPO′ ≡W C_N ⋆ LPO′ (monotonicity and associativity of ⋆, C_N ⋆ C_N ≡W C_N: all known to the engine).

proof.label: Lemma D
proof.text: Let Φ, Ψ witness g ≤_W D²₂. Let y ∈ dom(g), N ∈ ℕ, and let O_0, …, O_{r−1} be open sets of Baire space such that every name of every element of g(y) lies in some O_j. Then there are j < r, T ∈ ℕ and a finite family 𝒦 of pairs (F, m), with ∅ ≠ F ⊆ (N, m), such that (a) for every (F, m) ∈ 𝒦, every x ⊇ y|T and every set H′ with H′ ∩ [0,m) = F for which Ψ(x, H′) is total: Ψ(x, H′) ∈ O_j; (b) for every B ⊆ ℕ there is (F, m) ∈ 𝒦 with F ⊆ B or F ∩ B = ∅.

steps: Let A = A_{Φ(y)} and let X be A if A is infinite, its complement otherwise; put X_N = X ∩ (N, ∞). Every infinite H ⊆ X_N is a solution of Φ(y), so Ψ(y, H) is a name of an element of g(y).

H ↦ Ψ(y, H) is continuous on the infinite subsets of X_N, so the sets {H : Ψ(y,H) ∈ O_j} are open and "the least j with Ψ(y,H) ∈ O_j" is a finite Borel partition. If r = 1 put X′ = X_N and j = 0; otherwise the Galvin–Prikry theorem gives an infinite X′ ⊆ X_N and j such that Ψ(y, H) ∈ O_j for all infinite H ⊆ X′.

For each infinite H ⊆ X′, some finite prefix w of Ψ(y, H) has [w] ⊆ O_j; it is produced with some use (t, m), and we may take m > min H. Let 𝔽 be the set of all triples (F, m, t) so obtained, F = H ∩ [0,m) ≠ ∅, F ⊆ (N, m). For (F, m, t) ∈ 𝔽, x ⊇ y|t and H′ ∩ [0,m) = F, the output Ψ(x, H′) extends w, so lies in O_j if total.

Compactness. Suppose that for every finite 𝒦 ⊆ 𝔽 some B ⊆ ℕ splits every member (meets F and misses part of F). The sets {B ∈ 2^ℕ : B splits F} are clopen, so by compactness of 2^ℕ some B splits every F with (F, m, t) ∈ 𝔽. One of X′ ∩ B, X′ ∖ B is infinite; call it H. Then H ∩ [0,m) = F for some (F, m, t) ∈ 𝔽, and F ⊆ B or F ∩ B = ∅: a contradiction. So there is a finite 𝒦 ⊆ 𝔽 satisfying (b); let T be the largest t occurring in it. Then (a) holds by step 3.

proof.label: Corollary D
proof.text: In the situation of [#Lemma D], let x ∈ dom(g), x ⊇ y|T, be such that no element of g(x) has a name in O_j. Then A_{Φ(x)} or its complement is finite, and the finite one contains F for some (F, m) ∈ 𝒦; in particular it has an element > N.
proof: Apply (b) to B = A_{Φ(x)}: F ⊆ B or F ⊆ ℕ∖B for some (F, m) ∈ 𝒦; let Z be that side. If Z were infinite, H′ = F ∪ (Z ∩ [m, ∞)) would be a solution of Φ(x) with H′ ∩ [0,m) = F, so Ψ(x, H′) would be a name of an element of g(x), lying in O_j by (a): impossible.

proof.label: Theorem
proof.text: LPO′ ≰_W D²₂.

steps: Let II : 2^ℕ → 2 be II(x) = 1 iff x has infinitely many ones. II ≤_sW LPO′: map x to the sequence p_s = 0^{k_s} 1 0^ω, where k_s is the number of ones in x|s. If x has exactly k ones, p_s is eventually 0^k 1 0^ω ≠ 0^ω; if x has infinitely many, p_s → 0^ω. So LPO(lim p_s) = II(x). It suffices to show II ≰_W D²₂.

Suppose Φ, Ψ witness II ≤_W D²₂. Build σ_0 ⊆ σ_1 ⊆ … in 2^{<ω}: σ_0 = ∅. Given σ_i, let y_i = σ_i 0^ω, so II(y_i) = 0. Apply [#Lemma D] with y = y_i, N = i, r = 1 and O_0 = the names of the answer 0. It gives T_i and 𝒦_i. Let σ_{i+1} = (y_i | max(T_i, |σ_i|)) 1.

Let x = ⋃ σ_i. It has infinitely many ones, so II(x) = 1 has no name in O_0, and x ⊇ y_i|T_i for every i. By [#Corollary D], for every i one of A_{Φ(x)}, ℕ∖A_{Φ(x)} is finite and has an element > i. Both sets cannot be finite, so it is the same finite set Z for all i, and Z has an element > i for every i: a contradiction.

blocks.label: Sort ≰_W D²₂ and C_I ≰_W D²₂ (hence IVT ≰_W D²₂; none of them below General-SADC)
proof: Proof for Sort.

steps: Suppose Φ, Ψ witness Sort ≤_W D²₂. Let σ_0 = ∅. Given σ_i with k_i zeros, let y_i = σ_i 1^ω, so Sort(y_i) = 0^{k_i} 1^ω. Apply [#Lemma D] with y_i, N = i, r = 1, O_0 = [0^{k_i} 1]; get T_i, 𝒦_i. Let σ_{i+1} = (y_i | max(T_i, |σ_i|)) 0.
x = ⋃ σ_i has infinitely many zeros, Sort(x) = 0^ω ∉ O_0 for every i. Conclude as in section 5, step 3. Proof for C_I.

Suppose Φ, Ψ witness C_I ≤_W D²₂. Build rational intervals I_0 = [0,1] ⊇ I_1 ⊇ … of positive length and finite strings σ_0 ⊆ σ_1 ⊆ …, where σ_i enumerates finitely many rational open intervals with union [0,1] ∖ I_i (σ_0 is empty; a symbol "no ball" is available for padding).

Given σ_i and I_i = [a, b], ℓ = b − a, let y_i be σ_i followed by padding: a name of I_i. Fix n with 2^{−n} < ℓ/6, and let O_0 = {names (q_k) with q_n < (a+b)/2}, O_1 = {names with q_n ≥ (a+b)/2}, two clopen sets covering all names. [#Lemma D] with y_i, N = i, r = 2 gives j, T_i, 𝒦_i.

If j = 0 let I_{i+1} = [a + 2ℓ/3, b]; if j = 1 let I_{i+1} = [a, a + ℓ/3]. A real r with a name in O_0 satisfies r ≤ q_n + 2^{−n} < a + 2ℓ/3; one with a name in O_1 satisfies r ≥ q_n − 2^{−n} > a + ℓ/3. So no point of I_{i+1} has a name in O_j. Let σ_{i+1} be y_i | max(T_i, |σ_i|) followed by codes of rational open intervals covering exactly I_i ∖ I_{i+1} within [0,1].
x = ⋃ σ_i enumerates the complement of ⋂ I_i = {r}, a legitimate instance (a = b). For every i, x ⊇ y_i | T_i and r ∈ I_{i+1} has no name in O_{j_i}. Conclude as in section 5, step 3.

blocks.label: LPO′, Sort and C_I are not Weihrauch reducible to ADC

proof.label: Lemma D′ (Lemma D for other problems, and for partitions into r′ pieces)
proof.text: Let 𝖯 be a problem whose solutions are infinite subsets of ℕ and such that every instance has a solution X all of whose infinite subsets are solutions. Let Φ, Ψ witness g ≤_W 𝖯, and y, N, O_0, …, O_{r−1} as in [#Lemma D], and r′ ≥ 1. Then there are j < r, T and a finite family 𝒦 of pairs (F, m), ∅ ≠ F ⊆ (N, m), with (a) as in [#Lemma D] and (b′): for every partition of ℕ into r′ pieces, some (F, m) ∈ 𝒦 has F inside one piece.

proof: Proof: as for [#Lemma D], with X as in the hypothesis in step 1, and 2^ℕ replaced by r′^ℕ in step 4 (one of the r′ sets X′ ∩ piece is infinite).
For ADC the hypothesis holds: an infinite linear order has an infinite ascending chain or an infinite descending chain X, and every infinite subset of X is a chain of the same kind.

proof.label: Lemma E (dead finite sets in a linear order)
proof.text: Let L be a linear order on ω. Let U be the set of e such that {z : z >_L e} has no infinite ascending chain, and W the set of e such that {z : z <_L e} has no infinite descending chain. (1) If F is finite, nonempty, F ⊆ [0,m) and F ∩ U = ∅, there is an infinite ascending chain C with C ∩ [0,m) = F. Symmetrically if F ∩ W = ∅, with a descending chain. (2) U ∩ W is finite.
proof: (1) Let u = max_L F. Since u ∉ U there is an infinite ascending chain C′ above u; let C = F ∪ (C′ ∩ [m, ∞)). An element of F has its C-predecessors inside F; an element of C′ has as C-predecessors elements of F and of C′, finitely many. So C is an infinite ascending chain and C ∩ [0,m) = F.
If e <_L e′ are in U ∩ W, the interval (e, e′) has no infinite ascending chain (e ∈ U) and no

infinite descending chain (e′ ∈ W), so it is finite. If U ∩ W were infinite, fix e in it; infinitely many elements of U ∩ W lie on one side of e, say above. They form an infinite set in which every element has finitely many predecessors above e, i.e. an infinite ascending chain above e, contradicting e ∈ U. Symmetrically below, contradicting e ∈ W.

proof.label: Corollary E
proof.text: Let Φ, Ψ witness g ≤_W ADC, and let j, T, 𝒦 be given by Lemma D′ with r′ = 4. If x ∈ dom(g), x ⊇ y|T and no element of g(x) has a name in O_j, then some (F, m) ∈ 𝒦 has F ⊆ U ∩ W, where U, W are computed in L = Φ(x).
proof: Apply (b′) to the partition {U ∩ W, U ∖ W, W ∖ U, ℕ ∖ (U ∪ W)}: some F lies in one piece. If the piece is not U ∩ W, then F ∩ U = ∅ or F ∩ W = ∅, and Lemma E(1) gives a solution C of L with C ∩ [0,m) = F; by (a), Ψ(x, C) is a name in O_j of an element of g(x): impossible.

proof.label: Theorem′
proof.text: LPO′ ≰_W ADC, Sort ≰_W ADC, C_I ≰_W ADC.
proof: Run the three constructions of sections 5 and 6 (same σ_i, y_i, O_j, N = i), using Lemma D′ with r′ = 4 instead of [#Lemma D]. For the limit instance x, [#Corollary E] gives for every i a nonempty F_i ⊆ U ∩ W with min F_i > i, where U ∩ W is computed in Φ(x). So U ∩ W is infinite, contradicting Lemma E(2).

items.dependencies: for r = 1 below (LPO′, Sort) none. For r = 2 (section 6) the Galvin–Prikry theorem (every finite Borel partition of the infinite subsets of an infinite set has an infinite homogeneous set), classical. Lemma D and Corollary D (section 5); the Galvin–Prikry theorem for C_I. the proof of Lemma D (section 5); every infinite linear order has an infinite suborder of type ω or ω* (classical); Galvin–Prikry for C_I only.
items.concerns: the commitment is made on y_i but used on x; legitimate because the computation reads only y_i|t and χ_F|m, and x ⊇ y_i|T. (ii) The set H′ = F ∪ (Z ∩ [m,∞)) really is a solution: F ⊆ Z and Z is A or its complement. (iii) F ≠ ∅ is arranged by taking m > min H, and F ⊆ (N, ∞) because H ⊆ X_N; without it the final contradiction would fail. (iv) Step 4 of the lemma is where one could go wrong: the family 𝔽 contains, for every infinite H ⊆ X′, an initial part of H, which is exactly what the compactness argument needs. (v) Sanity: the argument does not apply to LPO or C_ℕ (which are below D²₂): there the limit instance x does not contradict the commitments. It does not apply to SRT²₂ in place of D²₂, where a finite F homogeneous for the wrong colour is dead for another reason, consistent with section 3. for C_I the limit instance is a degenerate interval, so the argument says nothing about PCC (proper intervals). The clopen sets O_0, O_1 depend only on the n-th term of the name, so the partition of step 2 of Lemma D is clopen and only the clopen case of Galvin–Prikry (Nash-Williams) is used. for ADS a finite ascending *sequence* F cannot be continued downwards, so only U matters, U may be infinite (it is all of L when L has type k + ω*), and there is no contradiction; this is consistent with LPO′ ≤_W General-SADS ≤_W ADS. For chains, a finite set carries no direction, which is why both U and W are available and the partition into four pieces is needed. (ii) Lemma E(2): checked on L = ω + k + ω* (U ∩ W is the middle k) and on L = ω + ω* (empty). (iii) In Lemma D′, X is an ascending or descending chain of Φ(y), and all the commitments come from subsets of X; nothing about X is used in Φ(x). (iv) TC_ℕ, RT¹₂ × RT¹₂, C_ℕ are below ADC (sections 1, 11): for them the limit instance does not refute the commitments, so the construction does not start.
